chapters.title: Council staff opens hearing and gives instructions

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Hello, good morning.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Welcome to today's New York City Council hearing for the Committee on Economic Development, joint hearing with Transportation and Infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please silence all phones.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you wish to speak in today's hearing, please fill out on the parents'card with one of the sergeants.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Moving forward, no one is to approach the dais.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Chair, you may begin.

chapters.summary: Maloney welcomes attendees, notes co-chair Abreu, recognizes members, and states the focus on waterways and EDC assets.
chapters.title: Chair Maloney opens joint Economic Development and Transportation hearing

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: All right, good morning and welcome to this joint hearing of the New York City Council's Committees on Economic Development and Transportation and Infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: My name is Virginia Maloney and I have the privilege of serving as the chair of the Committee on Economic Development and I'm pleased to be joined by my co-chair, Majority Leader Sean Abreu.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Who chairs the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Before we begin, I'd like to note that we've been joined by a few council members, Council Member Aldebal, Council Member Farias, Council Member Riley, and Council Member Lewis.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Who is here as well.

chapters.summary: EDC runs NYC Ferry, oversees the East 23rd Street seaplane base, and controls berthing for excursion vessels at city-owned piers.
chapters.title: Maloney outlines EDC's role in ferries, seaplanes, and excursion vessels

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Today we are looking at how New Yorkers travel on the city's waterways and the role EDC plays in managing them.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: EDC runs the New York City Ferry and also oversees the seaplane base at East 23rd Street.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: It controls berthing for the excursion vessels at city-owned piers across the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: These are all city assets and they affect the neighborhoods around them every day.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: We want to understand today how EDC manages those assets and how it holds operators accountable when things go wrong.

chapters.summary: The system carried 7.4 million trips, cost $88 million to operate, brought in $27 million, and had an $8.33 subsidy per trip; base fare rose to $5.
chapters.title: Maloney details NYC Ferry ridership, costs, and fare increase

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: First, we'll be discussing ferries.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: New York City Ferry has become an important part of how New Yorkers get around.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: The system carried 7.4 million trips last fiscal year, and this summer the city ran the most ferry service in its history.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: In December, EDC launched the first major system-wide redesign of the routes since the system began, and this fall, New York City Ferry expanded discount fares to middle school students.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And we all enjoyed the FIFA-wrapped boats this summer.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: However, the New York City ferry system is very expensive to run.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: In fiscal year 2025, the system cost $88 million to operate and brought in about $27 million, which puts EDC's subsidy at $8.33 per trip.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And that figure does not include capital costs or the depreciation of the boats themselves.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: As of yesterday, riders are now paying more, with the base fare rising from $4.5 to $5.

chapters.summary: The contract worth up to $405 million expires in September 2028; the city must decide whether to renew, seek new bids, or try another model.
chapters.title: Maloney warns ferry operating contract expires in 2028

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: The biggest decision ahead is the operating contract.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: New York City Ferry is run by a private operator under an agreement worth up to $405 million.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And this agreement is expiring in September 2028.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: The last procurement process took about a year, so the city will have to decide very soon whether or not they plan to renew the current operator, seek new bids, or try something altogether different.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: The city owns the boats, so every option is on the table.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: We want to know how the operator has performed, what the city has received in advertising and other revenue, and how EDC is planning the next phase of the New York City ferry.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: A decision of this size should not be made without the council and the public at the table.

chapters.summary: A July 5 hard landing required FDNY evacuation; residents face regular noise and traffic; the city owns the facility and can set rules.
chapters.title: Maloney raises seaplane safety and noise concerns on East River

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Second,

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Sea planes are an issue that hits close to home for the Eastside communities that I represent.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: On July 5th of this year, a seaplane carrying eight people made a hard landing in the East River right off the base at East 23rd Street, snapping a wing strut.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: The FDNY had to take passengers off the plane.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thankfully, no one was seriously hurt, but it was not the first incident on the East River, and residents along the waterfront are living with regular noise and traffic of these flights.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I understand the federal government regulates aviation and the city cannot set the flight paths, but the city owns the facility and therefore can set reasonable rules for how it is used.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: EDC did that just 10 years ago at the downtown Manhattan heliport when it cut tourist helicopter flights in half and ended them on Sundays.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And when this council passed Local Law 64 last year to rein in noisy helicopters, seaplanes were not covered.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: We want to know who EDC has agreements with at the seaplane base, what the city gets in return, and whether EDC is prepared to use the tools it already has to work with the council and Eastside communities to better regulate these planes.

chapters.summary: Recent collisions near 23rd Street and West 125th Street injured dozens; a fatal capsizing near the Statue of Liberty involved an overloaded boat.
chapters.title: Maloney highlights party boat collisions and unlicensed charters

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Third, party boats raise many of the same concerns.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: In August 2025, a party boat carrying 300 people collided with another vessel on the East River near the 23rd Street landing, sending seven people to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: In June 2025, a party yacht with 400 people aboard struck a dock near West 125th Street, injuring 35.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Unlicensed charters have been even more dangerous.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: This August, a mother and her five-month-old daughter were killed when a boat carrying more passengers than it could legally hold capsized near the Statue of Liberty.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: The city has acted before.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: In 2019, it stopped party boats from boarding in Sheepshead Bay after repeated complaints from residents.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So we want to know what EDC requires of these operators before it lets them dock, whether anyone checks their Coast Guard credentials, and what happens when something goes wrong.

chapters.summary: Bills would establish or study ferry service at Canarsie Pier, Willets Point, West 125th Street, and City Island.
chapters.title: Maloney introduces four ferry expansion bills

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Today we are also hearing four bills that would require ferry service or a study of ferry service at Canarsie Pier, at Willits Point, at West 125th Street, and City Island.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: These bills reflect real demand from communities that want to be connected to the rest of the city by water.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I'll leave it to my co-chair and the bill's sponsors to speak to the legislation.

chapters.summary: Maloney recognizes Senior Counsel Alex Polonov, William Honak, and Spencer Kuhn, then yields to Majority Leader Abreu.
chapters.title: Maloney thanks committee staff and turns to co-chair

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Before we begin, I want to recognize the Economic Development Committee staff for their work in preparing for today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you to Senior Counsel Alex Polonov, Senior Policy Analyst William Honak, and Financial Analyst Spencer Kuhn.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I'll now turn the floor over to my co-chair, Majority Leader Sean Abreu, for his opening remarks.

chapters.summary: Abreu thanks Maloney and says waterways are an integral but often overlooked part of transportation and the economy.
chapters.title: Majority Leader Abreu opens Transportation Committee remarks

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Maloney.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Good morning and welcome to today's joint hearing.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I am Council Member Sean Abreu, Majority Leader and Chair of the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I would like to thank Chair Maloney for joining me in today's hearing.

chapters.summary: Staten Island Ferry serves over 16 million passengers annually; NYC Ferry has 38 vessels, six routes, 25 landings, and over 7 million trips per year.
chapters.title: Abreu cites Staten Island Ferry and NYC Ferry scale

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: New York City's waterways are an integral yet often overlooked part of our transportation network and our economy.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Every day, they support public and private ferry services, commercial and recreational vessels, freight movement, and seaplane operations.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: New York City's ferry systems are particularly noteworthy.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The Staten Island Ferry is the busiest municipal ferry service in the country.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: serving over 16 million passengers annually, 24 hours a day, 365 days a year.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And the New York City Ferry, with 38 vessels across six routes and 25 landings, makes over 7 million trips per year and is the largest passenger-only ferry fleet in the country.

chapters.summary: The 2025 Optimization Plan reconfigured the network; Abreu wants affordable, reliable, accessible service and lessons for the future.
chapters.title: Abreu discusses ferry optimization and accessibility goals

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: These systems have made improvements over the years, but there is still a need to make the systems more affordable, reliable, and accessible.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The City's 2025 New York City Ferry Optimization Plan was an important step toward addressing some of these issues.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The plan reconfigured the ferry network to improve connections and make service more efficient.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Today, we want to understand what those changes accomplished, what the administration has learned, and how those lessons can inform the future of the system.

chapters.summary: Abreu says ferry can fill transit gaps, support housing density, and strengthen commercial corridors; West Harlem has waterfront infrastructure.
chapters.title: Abreu introduces Intro 1022 for West 125th Street ferry

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: For many waterfront communities, ferry service has the potential to fill much-needed gaps in transportation, especially where access to the subway system is limited.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: It would allow for additional means of accessible transit, support additional housing density, and strengthen local commercial corridors.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: That is why I introduced introduction number 1022 to establish regular ferry service at or near West 125th Street.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: West Harlem already has waterfront infrastructure and connections to the surrounding transportation network that could be leveraged to better connect this community.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: to the rest of the city.

chapters.summary: Abreu thanks Jaleesa Quigley, Jake Borey, Sierra Townsend, Theodore Miller, Kevin Katowski, John Bazile, and Richard Yates-Wong.
chapters.title: Abreu thanks staff and yields to Council Member Farias

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you to my staff and committee staff for their hard work in preparing for today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Jaleesa Quigley, my Deputy Chief of Staff, Jake Borey, my Senior Advisor, Sierra Townsend, Senior Legislative Counsel, Theodore Miller, Legislative Counsel,

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Kevin Katowski, Senior Policy Analyst, John Bazile, Senior Policy Analyst, and Richard Yates-Wong, Finance Analyst.

chapters.summary: Farias thanks chairs and co-sponsors Aldebol, Riley, and Sanchez, and reflects on four years as Economic Development chair expanding ferry service.
chapters.title: Council Member Farias introduces Intro 1032 for City Island ferry

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I will now turn it over to Council Member Farias for her opening.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you both to Chairs Maloney and Abreu for convening today's joint hearing and providing the opportunity to speak on my legislation, Intro 1032.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I want to also thank my co-prime sponsor and sponsors of the bill, Council Members Shirley Aldable, Kevin Riley, and Justin Sanchez for their partnership and commitment to expanding transportation opportunities for our communities in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: For four years, I served as chair of the Committee on Economic Development, where I worked hard to expand NYC ferry service and bring more landings throughout our city, including along the east side of the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Can we make sure all mics are off?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I pushed to make ferry service more accessible to middle and high school students, advocated for greater language access, and held hearings on how we could use our waterways to promote tourism and create new revenue-generating opportunities for our city,

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: among many other oversight topics you folks are familiar with.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: That experience reinforced my belief that our waterways are an underutilized resource for transportation, economic development, and connecting communities.

chapters.summary: City Island has one way in and out, more than 20 vacant storefronts, and needs ferry service to boost businesses and provide commuting options.
chapters.title: Farias describes City Island's transit isolation and vacant storefronts

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Today, I am bringing that same commitment to City Island.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Since 2023, residents have reached out to my office about the possibility of ferry service to City Island.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I have spoken with residents and local business owners, and as someone who has lived in the Bronx my entire life and regularly spends time on the island, I understand both its unique character and the challenges that come with getting there.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: City Island is one of the Bronx's most distinctive destinations with a rich maritime history, waterfront restaurants, fishing opportunities, and independent businesses that contribute to our borough's identity.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Yet, access to the island remains heavily dependent on traveling by car or bus, with one way in and one way out, might I add.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Earlier this year, News 12 reported that more than 20 storefronts on City Island were vacant, and many of those have remained vacant for decades.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: This should give us pause.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: We need to ask what more New York City can do to support these commercial corridors.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: attract customers, and create opportunities for businesses to thrive.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Ferry service should be an integral part of that conversation.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: A connection to the citywide ferry network yields that promise of a broader customer base to the city islands, restaurants, shops, and waterfront attractions.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: It could also provide residents with another transportation option for commuting and accessing essential services while giving visitors an alternative to driving taxis or limited bus service.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: We should be looking for ways to support economic activity without requiring every additional visitor to arrive by car.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Improved transit access presents an opportunity to strengthen local businesses while examining ways to ease our roadway congestion.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: My office has heard directly from Bronxites and City Islanders alike, all who want the city to explore this possibility.

chapters.summary: Farias says 350 emails support the bill and 8 oppose it; Intro 1032 requires a feasibility study and a process for site selection, design, and construction.
chapters.title: Farias cites support for City Island ferry and clarifies bill scope

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: To date, we have currently received over 350 emails and letters in support of expanding ferry service to City Island, including

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: from folks on the City Island Rising membership and other individual supporters, with the majority representing supporters of this legislation.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: In comparison, to date, I have received eight expressions of opposition and or amendments to this legislation.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: The level of support we have received from the people who have personally taken the time to engage with my office on this proposal underscores the importance of evaluating all potential benefits through this comprehensive feasibility study.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: We must listen to concerns and consider the potential impacts, but we must also recognize

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: the interest in exploring a transportation investment that could benefit residents, businesses, and visitors alike.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And while I have the opportunity, I want to clarify the scope of Intro 1032.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I encourage everyone to read the bill in its entirety because this legislation calls for the evaluation of potential landing sites on or adjacent to City Island.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: If a suitable location is identified, the bill also establishes a process for site selection, design, and construction with ferry service to follow upon completion.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: While previous administrations and the New York City Economic Development Corporation has studied City Island and Orchard Beach and reached their own determinations, we should continue exploring broader waterfront

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: broader waterfronts given the success we have had with ferry service at Soundview and Ferry Point Park.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: We should not assume that the existing ferry network, including the Soundview and Ferry Point landings, represents the full extent of what is possible for the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: We need to evaluate additional waterfront opportunities and consider their potential transportation, economic, environmental, and tourism benefits.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: That's precisely why a feasibility study is necessary to understand which locations may be suitable, what infrastructure and investment would be required, how ferry service could affect

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: local businesses and commuters, and what environmental considerations we can address along the way.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: In the interest of making informed decisions based on evidence and community input, I have drafted Intro 1032 to effectively fulfill that.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And before I conclude, I do want to reinforce a few important points about the scope and intent of Intro 1032.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: The legislation does not predetermine a ferry landing location.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: It requires the city to evaluate potential sites on or adjacent to City Island, considering their feasibility and impacts on the surrounding community.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Critically, it goes beyond a study by establishing a process for site selection, design, construction, and ultimately ferry service if a suitable location is identified.

chapters.summary: Farias wants perspectives from residents, businesses, and advocates; the bill does not predetermine a location and should center affected communities.
chapters.title: Farias welcomes testimony and urges community voice

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: As we hear testimony today, I welcome the perspectives of residents, business owners, advocates, and other stakeholders.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I also look forward to hearing from how we can strengthen this legislation to ensure

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: that the communities most affected have a voice in the process.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I'm proud to champion Intro 1032 because waterfront communities deserve thoughtful consideration, better connectivity, and opportunities for economic growth.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: After four years of working to expand our city's ferry network, I know that we must continue asking where ferry service can go next and how our waterways can be better serve the people who live, work, and do business along them.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Aldebol introduces Intro 1030-2026 for a study of ferry service to City Island and seeks data on East Bronx transit needs.
chapters.title: Council Member Aldebol introduces City Island ferry study bill

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'd like to recognize that we've been joined by Hanif on Zoom, Thomas Henry, Marte, Jay Sanchez, Banks, and De La Rosa, Councilmember Aldebar, followed by Thomas Henry for your openings.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Abreu.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I'm happy to be here today to discuss the importance of our waterfronts and the opportunities we have to study and expand ferry service across the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I want to thank my colleagues, Majority Leader Abreu, Chair Maloney for holding this hearing, and my colleague, Councilmember Farias, Kevin Riley, and Justin Sanchez for their partnership.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Earlier this fall, Councilmember Farias and I introduced Intro 1030-2026 requiring a study on the feasibility and utility of expanding New York City Ferry Service to the City Island area.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: The goal of this legislation is to gain more accurate and relevant data on the transit patterns and needs of the East Bronx residents, as well as updated information on the logistical feasibility of additional ferry service in that area.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: The information provided by a new comprehensive study would help identify key considerations shedding light on economic activity, community vitality, and other factors needed to determine whether ferry service should be expanded.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: City Island is an incredibly special community, which I have the honor of representing on the City Council.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Expanded New York City ferry service in the area have the potential to be truly transformative for families, commuters, and small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: With the status quo, the city island that we know and love is being lost year after year as historic restaurants close their doors.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: doors and businesses close their doors and the next generation of families struggle to commute to work and to school while remaining on the island.

chapters.summary: Aldebol visited City Island with SBS Commissioner Minaya and saw vacant storefronts; Heart Island is only accessible through City Island.
chapters.title: Aldebol highlights empty storefronts and Heart Island access

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Earlier this year, I took SBS Commissioner Kenny Minaya to City Island to meet with local business owners.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: But the most striking part of that visit wasn't our conversations with the incredible family business owners or the delicious seafood we sampled.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: It was the empty storefronts we walked by, one after the other, right down City Island Avenue.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Another important constituency to consider in these discussions are those who have family and loved ones laid to rest on Heart Island.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: New York City has made significant strides in improving the accessibility of Heart Island and recognizing its complex history.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: However, the only way to Heart Island is through City Island, and for New Yorkers across the five boroughs, right now it is an incredibly difficult and long journey to make via public transit.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: City Island deserves to be a destination for its beautiful views, shopping, incredible food, bringing desperately needed traffic into the small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: But we also must make sure our efforts center the needs of City Island residents as well.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And from my engagement with City Island community, I understand that this issue is nuanced for many residents.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: A new study will provide critical context for future actions, helping us develop a plan based on data and community input.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I look forward to hearing more from EDC, the community members at today's hearing, so that we can work towards a plan that serves the best interests of City Island and the East Bronx.

chapters.summary: Willets Point is transforming with 2,500 affordable units, a soccer stadium, and jobs; the 7 train cannot carry the new neighborhood alone.
chapters.title: Council Member Thomas-Henry introduces Intro 846 for Willets Point ferry

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Councilmember Thomas Henry.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs Abreu and Maloney.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: What we are witnessing right now is one of the most transformative developments in Queens history.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: 2,500 units of affordable, 100% affordable housing, a new public school, thousands of jobs, new open spaces,

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: New York City's first soccer stadium at the odd park, a baseball stadium, a tennis stadium, and an airport, bringing thousands of fans and travelers and new academic opportunities to our borough.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Despite all of this, Willits Point is still defined by its potential and one slogan.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: One way in, one way out.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We cannot build a community of the future while leaving it dependent on the current transportation infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: The 7 train has been the lifeline of this corridor.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And while it has served generations of New Yorkers, we cannot keep expecting one subway line to carry the weight of an entirely new neighborhood

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: thousands of new residents, and millions of visitors traveling to Citi Field, Etihad Park, the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Open, and the proposed Metropolitan Park de

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Intro 846 is legislation that would expand ferry service between Woollett's Point and Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: It's a common sense solution to our ever-growing community.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry notes 33,000 fans per Mets game, 25,000 seats at Etihad Park, and 2,500 homes; ferry would provide an alternative and support local businesses.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry cites Mets, Etihad Park, and housing numbers

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I mean, let's just look at the numbers.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And as a daughter of Queens, you know I have to start with the New York Mets.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: This season alone, the Mets welcomed an average of over 33,000 fans on any given game day to Citi Field.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And that's in a losing season.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Now let's add to that equation 25,000 seats at Etihad Park, 2,500 affordable homes,

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thousands of permanent jobs and colleagues, that doesn't even begin to account for the proposed Metropolitan Park development.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: That equals greater pressure on the same infrastructure that our communities already depend on.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And who feels that pressure?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Our neighbors, our working families, and our small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: The math is not complicated.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: If we are going to multiply the number of people coming to Willits Point, we must expand ways they can get there.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: That is what Intro 846 is about.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: A future where a family living in Willits Point has more than one reliable way to get to work.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Where a Mets fan or NYCFC supporter can spend time supporting our local restaurants, shops, and small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And where transportation is not an afterthought, but a foundation of responsible growth for our neighbors in Corona,

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: East Elmhurst, Flushing, and the surrounding communities.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We cannot build world-class destinations with one way in and one way out.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Intro 846 is about planning for the Queens we are building, protecting the quality of life of the neighbors who built it, and making sure that growth works for everyone.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Wong is Executive Director of NYC Ferry at EDC; he is joined by Anton Fredrickson, Michelle Lamberti, and John Regan from DOT.
chapters.title: James Wong introduces EDC ferry team and colleagues

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Maloney, Majority Leader Abreu, members of the Committee on Economic Development, and members of the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: My name is James Wong, and I'm an Executive Vice President and serve as Executive Director of NYC Ferry at the New York City Economic Development Corporation.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: I'm joined today by my colleagues Anton Fredrickson, Senior Vice President and Head of Ports, Waterfront, and Transportation, and Michelle Lamberti, Vice President of Government and Community Partnerships, and John Regan from the Department of Transportation.

chapters.summary: The system has carried 56 million passengers since 2017 and set a single-day record on August 15 with nearly 57,000 riders; 94% of riders are NYC residents.
chapters.title: Wong touts NYC Ferry 50 millionth rider and record ridership

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: At its core, NYC Ferry connects New Yorkers to the city's vast waterfront area.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Waterfront opportunity.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: across all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Our work advances the Mamdani administration's commitment to economic justice by ensuring that transportation and public spaces are more accessible, affordable, and inclusive.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: As Deputy Mayor for Economic Justice, Julie Hsu has emphasized, affordability means creating the conditions for people to live good lives with more quality time, connection, and joy.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: As our waterfront grows, we must ensure these public investments continue to benefit all New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Earlier this year, NYC Ferry reached a huge milestone, our 50 millionth rider.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Today, the system has carried more than 56 million passengers since launching in 2017.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: And this summer, NYC Ferries set single-day ridership records three times, including on August 15th, when nearly 57,000 passengers rode the system, the highest daily ridership in our system's history.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: That demand came during a major summer for New York City, with the FIFA World Cup, the Knicks Championship Parade, Sailforth 250, concerts, cultural events, beach days, fireworks, and neighborhood celebrations drawing people all across the city.

chapters.summary: FIFA World Cup, parades, concerts, and cultural events drew riders; ferry connects people to local businesses, jobs, and destinations.
chapters.title: Wong credits summer events for ferry demand and public benefit

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: And NYC Ferry was ready for it.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: These moments show what happens when transportation, public space, economic development, and culture come together.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: When someone steps off the ferry, they connect to local businesses, jobs, and destinations across the city, from the Lower East Side to the Rockaways, Astoria to the Upper East Side, Brooklyn to Staten Island, and Midtown to Governor's Island.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: That is the promise of a ferry system, supporting local economies, connecting waterfront communities, and New Yorkers to jobs and recreation.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: After all, our surveys indicate that 94% of our riders are New York City residents.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: That is the public benefit we are focused on, making ferry service work for riders, neighborhoods, and the city while being responsible stewards of public finances.

chapters.summary: The December overhaul was shaped by 15,000 riders; trips rose 6%, East 34th and Midtown West terminals rose 21%, and the East River route rose 17%.
chapters.title: Wong reports route redesign increased ridership and efficiency

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: That has meant looking at the system the way riders experience it, where they are trying to go, how long trips take, whether vessels have enough room, and how to ensure each route makes the best use of public dollars.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Last December, we put that work into action with the first system-wide route overhaul since NYC Ferry launched in 2017.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: The plan was shaped by feedback from more than 15,000 riders and focused on five practical goals, giving riders more direct access to Midtown and Lower Manhattan,

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: speeding up commutes, adding capacity during the busiest times, improving operational efficiency, and reducing the subsidy per rider by growing ridership with limited new costs.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Since implementing these changes and following a full summer of ridership, we can see it's working.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Between May 1st and September 15th, trips were up about 6% compared with the prior year.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Ridership at the East 34th Street and Midtown West 39th Street terminals increased by 21%, showing strong demand for Midtown connections.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: The East River route, our most popular, saw a 17% increase after we added capacity and shortened travel times.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: And roughly 9% of overall ridership now comes from connections that didn't exist under the old network.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: That kind of growth is important not only because New Yorkers are using the system, but because it shows how smarter service planning

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: can improve access while making every public dollar work harder.

chapters.summary: FY26 subsidy is $8.79, down from a peak near $13; NYC Ferry has the lowest subsidy per rider among major publicly funded passenger ferry systems.
chapters.title: Wong reports $8.79 per-rider subsidy, below national peers

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: That brings us to the financial side of the system.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Like every public transit system, NYC Ferry depends on public subsidy, and our focus is ensuring that investment delivers more public benefit, more access, better service, and stronger connections across the city.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Our FY26 financials were recently finalized, and our per-rider subsidy is $8.79, remaining more than 30% below its fiscal 20 peak of nearly $13.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: With a subsidy under $9, NYC Ferry continues to have the lowest subsidy per rider of any major publicly funded passenger ferry system in the nation.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Our subsidy provider is also lower than many other forms of local and regional transit, including MTA Express Bus Service, Long Island Railroad, and Metro North.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Despite cost pressures from fuel, inflation, and optimized services, the broader direction on subsidy remains healthy.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Ridership is growing, fare box revenue is up, and we expect the route changes to keep paying off.

chapters.summary: Discount participation nearly doubled to 30,000 riders; base fare rose to $5, the 10-trip pass to $30, and the discount fare to $1.50.
chapters.title: Wong details discount program and fare changes

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Affordability is central to our financial approach to the system.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Through the NYC Ferry Discount Program, we are working to ensure that all New Yorkers can access the system.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: The program provides discounts off our lowest priced tickets to seniors, students, people with disabilities, and anyone eligible for the Fair Fares NYC program.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Participation has nearly doubled since 2024 to about 30,000 riders, and customers used roughly 230,000 discounted tickets last year, helping more New Yorkers ride NYC Ferry.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: This year, we built on that community.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: by extending discounted weekday ferry trips to middle school students.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: NYC Ferry's commitment to equitable access guided the fare changes that took effect yesterday, protecting affordability for regular riders, student, and discount users, while ensuring the system can keep delivering broader public benefits with healthy finances.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Our base fare increased from $4.50 to $5, remaining well below the MTA Express fare at $7.25, and in line with a 30-minute non-electric city bike ride.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: For frequent riders, the 10-trip pass increased from $29 to $30.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: For discount program participants, the fare increased by just $0.05 from $1.45 to $1.50.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: This approach focuses the largest increase on occasional riders and visitors who have shown that they are willing to pay more for the service, while protecting access for those who rely on it most.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: It also helps ensure the public subsidy continues to support broader benefits.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Shorter travel times, less congestion, reliable access to jobs, schools, and waterfront neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: And waterfront neighborhoods.

chapters.summary: EDC is replacing engines, building a swing barge and Atlantic Basin home port, replacing ticketing machines, and starting East 34th Street terminal redesign.
chapters.title: Wong outlines infrastructure investments and East 34th redesign

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: But fares are only one part of keeping the system sustainable.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We also have to keep investing in the physical infrastructure, vessels, landings, and customer experience that riders depend on every day.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: As NYC Ferry approaches its 10th year, we are investing in the repairs and upgrades needed to keep service safe, reliable, and ready for the future.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: As a starting point, we are improving air quality emissions by starting a major engine replacement project across our largest vessels in the fleet.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Looking to our infrastructure, we are building a swing barge to support main

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: on our many landings, constructing a necessary warehousing and home port facility in Atlantic Basin, Breadhook, replacing ticketing machines to improve the customer experience, and preparing for the long-term overhaul of vessels.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We are also kicking off discussions around redesign and community needs at the East 34th Street Terminal.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: As the second busiest passenger terminal in the system, the aging facility is increasingly constrained by major limitations.

chapters.summary: The ferry system has provided alternate service during Staten Island disruptions, rescued people in the water, and works with NYC Emergency Management.
chapters.title: Wong says ferry system supports emergency response

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Maintaining a strong and resilient system is about more than getting people from one place to another.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: It's also about making sure the city has the capacity to respond when emergencies happen, whether during severe storms, subway service disruptions, or mass evacuations.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Our ferry system has provided alternate services during Staten Island ferry disruptions, rescued people in the water, and works closely with the New York City Emergency Management to help keep New Yorkers safe on and around the waterfront.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: These investments are critical to ensure that we're maintaining and improving the service that exists today and must be considered alongside conversations discussing system growth.

chapters.summary: EDC released its 2025 Ferries Report and is developing a vision study to explore ferry service through NYC Ferry or other funding and operating models.
chapters.title: Wong describes 2025 Ferries Report and citywide vision study

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Last year, EDC released its 2025 Ferries Report, which laid out our plan to invest in key system-wide infrastructure and develop a broader vision study to comprehensively explore opportunities to bring ferry service to waterfront sites across New York City,

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: whether through NYC Ferry or other funding and operating models.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: This work is underway and we expect it will better address requests at scale.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: The council bills concerning ferry service at Canarsie, West 125th Street, and Willits Point, along with the bill on the feasibility study for City Island Ferry Service, raise important questions about transit access and waterfront connectivity.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We share these goals, particularly for communities underserved by existing transit.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: But expansion must be grounded in projected ridership, community needs, water conditions, infrastructure requirements, operating costs, and sustainable funding.

chapters.summary: Canarsie needs federal coordination and $30 million pier rehabilitation; West 125th needs vessels and upland improvements; Willets Point has mudflats and shallow water.
chapters.title: Wong details challenges at Canarsie, West 125th, and Willets Point

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: While we believe it is important to thoughtfully assess growth opportunities citywide, we have reviewed many of the requested sites, including where these council bills propose ferry service, and understand some of the challenges that they may face.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Canarsie, for example, falls within the Gateway National Recreation Area and Jamaica Bay, requiring federal coordination and National Park Service review.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: National Parks has previously indicated that they do not support commuter ferry uses on the pier.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Even if it did, the pier is in need of rehabilitation, last estimated at roughly $30 million.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: several years ago before any ferry infrastructure could be considered, funded, and built.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: West 125th Street would require additional vessels, operating funding, and improvements to support safe, accessible commuter operations.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Willits Point faces navigational access infrastructure challenges, including mudflats and shallow water conditions in Flushing Bay.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Challenging waterfront infrastructure, and the ongoing work of the Parks Department on marina and esplanade improvements at World's Fair Marina.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Finally, while there's a compatible barge at West 125th Street, it is over four miles outside of NYC Ferry's service area and would require new vessels to be built, operating funding, and upland improvements.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Unlike some other proposals, however, private ferry operators do operate nearby via New Jersey and could be an opportunity site for their future growth.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Our preliminary estimates show that the bills establishing new ferry service, plus the one for which a study was requested, as written, would require adding eight additional vessels to the fleet to run up to four new routes, resulting in $25 to $30 million

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: in annual operating expenses, an increase of more than 30% of NYC Ferry's overall budget.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Capital costs could reach hundreds of millions of dollars for upland improvements, vessels, queuing, and accessibility, and the new ferry landings themselves.

chapters.summary: Preliminary estimates show eight additional vessels, $25-30 million annual operating costs, and hundreds of millions in capital; the vision study is due summer 2027.
chapters.title: Wong says vision study should evaluate bills, cannot support legislation

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: While we share the underlying goal of improving waterfront access, we believe the vision study is the right vehicle for evaluating these proposals in a comprehensive data-driven way.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: The vision study is evaluating more than 40 waterfront

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: sites, including the sites in the council's proposed bills, along with other underserved communities.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: The study will give us the fact base to comprehensively evaluate waterfront sites, including the costs, ridership potential, infrastructure needs, water conditions, permitting requirements,

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: potential operating models, and a thoughtful consideration about whether service can be delivered through NYC Ferry, a private operator, a recreational model, or a different service approach.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: That work is underway and is expected to wrap up in summer of 2027.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: For that reason, we cannot support the proposed council legislation, but rather believe a responsible path forward is through the vision study in close consultation with city council.

chapters.summary: The seaplane base dates to the 1930s and averages 1,620 flights annually; Billy Bay Marina Services manages it under DOC NYC, with EDC oversight.
chapters.title: Wong describes Skyport seaplane base oversight

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: EDC also oversees the New York Skyport seaplane base at East 23rd Street.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: The facility dates to the late 1930s when it was developed under Mayor LaGuardia.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: It primarily supports by the seat and charter service, averaging 1,620 flights annually between 2016 and 2025.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Billy Bay Marina Services, the operator of the city's public piers program called DOC NYC, manages the seaplane base along with other piers and wharves across the city.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: EDC and the operator have worked to strengthen operating procedures, communication with East River Marine Traffic, and the Federal Aviation Administration, improving coordination with seaplane operators and industry stakeholders.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: This work includes improving pre-season coordination, public information, and preparing to rehabilitate the Skyport Marina, providing infrastructure and

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: improvements to reduce potential queuing in the East River.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: As the waterfront grows, our responsibility is to manage these assets transparently and safely while balancing mobility, jobs, and neighborhood quality of life.

chapters.summary: EDC manages piers for excursion vessels; DOC NYC handles permitting and safety; at Pier 36, measures include scheduling limits, security, and ticket seller enforcement.
chapters.title: Wong explains public piers program and Pier 36 improvements

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: As the steward of much of the city's waterfront, EDC manages New York City's public piers, docks, and wharves supporting excursion vessels, or boats that take passengers out for sightseeing, dining, cultural, educational, and recreation trips.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: It also supports offshore construction, tug-in barge operations, and other maritime activity.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Through the DOC NYC program, Billy Bay Marina Services manages day-to-day functions like permitting, scheduling, site coordination, and safety measures, while EDC retains oversight authority.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: At Pier 36, where excursion vessel activity has raised community concerns, EDC and DOC NYC have worked directly with Community Board 3, elected officials, and local stakeholders to improve operations.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Measures taken include advanced reservation and scheduling, limits on concentrated late-night departures, additional security, better spacing of arrivals and departures, coordination with nearby events, and improved drop-off management.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: DOC NYC, in consultation with EDC, also enforces prohibitions on unauthorized third-party street ticket sellers through investigations and follow-up with operators.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Substantiated violations can result in financial penalties and, for repeat violations, permit termination.

chapters.summary: Wong says the work aims to connect New Yorkers to the waterfront, support neighborhoods and small businesses, and welcomes questions.
chapters.title: Wong closes on waterfront access and NYC Ferry future

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Ultimately, all this work is about building New York City's connection to the waterfront and delivering a transportation system that reaches more New Yorkers, strengthens neighborhood connections, and works for both city major moments and everyday riders.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: It is also about making sure the energy generated by waterfront activities supports neighborhoods, small businesses, workers, and communities.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: New York's waterfront should be a place every New Yorker can reach, enjoy, work in, build a business in, and build a life around.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Not a place limited to those who can afford to live there or visit it.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: That is what we mean when we say transportation connects people to possibility.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: And that is the future we are building with NYC Ferry.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: I want to thank you for the opportunity to speak with you today, and we welcome any questions you have.

chapters.summary: Narcisse says Canarsie is a transit desert with one L train and packed buses; Intro 704 would establish regular ferry service and should be fast-tracked with housing.
chapters.title: Council Member Narcisse testifies on Canarsie Pier ferry bill

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Councilmember Narciso, you make your opening.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, for giving me the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I am here.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I just heard about $30 million for Canarsie Park, but I did not hear how much, you know, each specific other area.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I don't know how Canarsie already have the numbers, I guess because we've been fighting.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: On the fast track now for building, we are at the bottom 12, so there is plan to actually have more development in that area, right?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But right now, as we speak, it takes about an hour and some minutes to get here from that side of town to here.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I want to speak about my bill N274, which would require the city to establish regular ferry service at Canarsie Pier.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Canarsie is my hometown, and it is a transit desert.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We have one subway line at the very end of the L train, which is not inside the inlet of the community.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: The buses are packed.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I have a fellow that was traveling and never seen anything like that.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You have to squeeze yourself to get in any transportation, whether the train or the buses.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: People in my district can spend an hour and a half, like I said, to even from here to there.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And when the train goes down, there is nowhere else to turn.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I raised four children.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And to get to Manhattan, to get to LaGuardia, to get to Bronx Science,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: It was not easy.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And I know what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I'm talking about years, right?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So right now, it's going to be much more difficult, right?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: There's nowhere.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: L residents are thirsty for options.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We've been fighting for decades.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Canarsie had ferry service in the early 1900s.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And then now we're fighting for it to come back.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: My community has waited long enough for this return.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Now the city has put Community Board 18, like I said, on the fast track list.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: If we are bringing more housing to our area, we need infrastructure to match.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We have infrastructure problems in all aspects, and we're not having them addressed, but we're having more development.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: More homes mean more people who need to get to work, to school, and to doctors, and our transit is already stretched.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: If the city can fast-track housing in Canarsie, I am also asking it to fast-track this ferry too.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: A stop at Canarsie Pier would not only offer relief to commuters, but also bring visitors to Jamaica Bay.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I don't know if you heard about Churchillism and all the things that we have to offer, but there is no transportation to bring people in.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So we need that.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: It means customer.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I was training from small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We need business opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We're talking about economics, right?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So if you bring development, you have to bring everything that come with it.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You have to assess the school and the transit.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You know it's already dead.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So we need to address that.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: A ferry would bring life back to the waterfront and open the door to economic development our community has been asking for for decades.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Canarsie Pier is a city asset sitting right there, ready to be used.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We used to have a restaurant at the Canarsie Pier.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We used to have activities.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Now we have more people, less activities because we're not offering anything.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And it's an asset that we can use.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I am asking my colleagues to support this intro, 704.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I look forward to hearing not only from you to say what we're going to do.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I heard about the money part, but in the long run, if you have planned for development, you have to have that planned too because there is no transportation.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So that's all.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I rest my case, and I want to say thank you to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I got to run to my own hearing.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I apologize.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember, and thank you for that testimony.

chapters.summary: Maloney asks which aspects EDC versus DOT controls and where the largest gap is; Wong explains NYC Ferry is EDC-managed but DOT licenses private ferries.
chapters.title: Maloney asks EDC and DOT to clarify waterfront authority

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So we'll start diving into questions.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: We covered a lot of different types of transit.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: New York City's waterways supports a growing mix of ferries, excursions, commercial, aviation activity, but responsibility for all that activity is divided among EDC, DOT,

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: other city agencies, and of course, federal regulators.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: EDC manages the New York City Ferry, the East 23rd Street Seaplane Base, the Skyport Marina, and other agreements through private operators.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So can you go into a bit more detail about which aspects are controlled by EDC versus DOT, and where you see the largest gap in the city's authority today?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: I guess I'll start with just the NYC Ferry portion, and then I'll let my colleagues talk a little bit more about the different assets.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So NYC Ferry, which was started coming up on 10 years ago, is a creature of EDC because EDC was able to

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: build the landings for which it has responsibility over a number of waterfront properties and the sort of like expertise on providing management on landings.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So we have a lot of that.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So the landings at which NYC Ferry operates, many of them EDC is managing directly.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Also, our ability to stand up the system in terms of

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: of the vessels and the operator was something that we were able to get done.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: And so NYC Ferry is an operation that NYC Ferry manages, but it is a privately operated system that is subject to the rules and regulations that DOT has as some of its chartered responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So I guess I'll turn to John just on the DOT part, and then we can talk about...

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: I'm John Regan, Executive Director of Security and Private Ferry Operations at New York City DOT Ferry Division.

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: Primarily, we operate the Staten Island Ferry, but in terms of what James is speaking about for licensing private ferry operations, an operator like Hornblower New York, who runs NYC Ferry for EDC,

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: they come to DOT annually for a private ferry operator license, and we license the route and landings that they run under.

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: So that is our primary responsibility with private ferries.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: And I'm Anton Fredrickson at EDC, a leader of Ports, Waterfront, and Transportation Department.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: As part of that, we have a public piers program.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So we manage a number of assets across the city to make available for these excursion vessels, but also the industrial working waterfront of the New York Harbor.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: And those piers are managed by a private operator called DocNYC, also known as Billy Bay Marina Services.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: And they manage this program centrally and provide a lot of the services, but also the checks and has been increasingly responsive to

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: potential complaints that we've received over time, and we work to strengthen that through our birthing licenses with DocNYC and the operators.

chapters.summary: Fredrickson says operators must follow Coast Guard and FAA rules; DOC NYC checks licenses and can revoke for repeat violations; EDC focuses on infrastructure compliance.
chapters.title: Maloney questions compliance monitoring across waterfront

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And how do you monitor compliance across the waterfront portfolio?

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So depending, so with DocNYC, the operators have to first follow all U.S.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: Coast Guard regulations on the seaplanes.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: That's U.S.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: Coast Guard, but also FAA when in the air.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: And then DocNYC does its own checks that all the licenses and certifications are in place with each of those operators.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: We also monitor for potential violations, and there is a penalty system in place depending on the offense.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: There is even the possibility, for example, with third-party street ticket selling, that if you're found to commit the same violation twice, we do revoke that license.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: And yeah, so that really incentivizes strong behavior from the operators to not lose that access to the peers, which ultimately is a source of income for that business owner.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And do you see any gaps in the city's authority?

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: Within the city's authority, we have a strong, robust program in place.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: We focus on what we can control, which is the management of the infrastructure and the compliance of vessels or aircraft that access our infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: The regulation and safety of the vessels or the aircraft are up to federal regulators, and we defer to them.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: NYC Ferry uses third-party audits and contract KPIs for maintenance and safety; multiple layers ensure operator compliance.
chapters.title: Wong explains ferry oversight through audits and KPIs

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: On the ferry side, we look through at NYC Ferry through a couple of different lenses.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Similar to what Anton is talking about, we have several different levels.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So there are the regulatory pieces that are national through Coast Guard and things like that.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We also have third-party audits that we do regularly with our operator to make sure that they're abiding by all the rules and regulations and all the things that we are expecting out of them from a safety perspective.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We also do, as part of our contract, we also have a number of key performance indicators to make sure that we are keeping a close eye.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So everything like maintenance, do you maintain a vessel well?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We are tracking that very closely to make sure that all planned maintenance happens in accordance with our plans.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: These are the multiple ways that we are keeping an eye on safety and operations to make sure that things are happening the way we expect them to.

chapters.summary: Wong calls the system healthy; subsidy is down from $13 to under $9; fare policy is equitable; he is proud of improvements.
chapters.title: Maloney asks about ferry system's operational and financial health

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Since the majority of the bills that we're discussing today are focused on the ferry system, we'll ask some questions focused on that.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: How would you characterize the current state of the ferry system, the operational, financial, and infrastructure challenges that you're facing right now?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Thank you for the question and the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: I would consider our financials and the state of the system very healthy.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: I think that, you know, for those with longer memories, we did have times when the cost of NYC ferry had gotten expensive, and we've done a lot of work over the last several years to affect change here.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We've gone from a subsidy per rider of nearly $13 per rider to under $9.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: It's more than 30% decrease despite the intense inflationary pressures that we're facing around the country.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We've done things like we procure our contracts so that we have a really effective instrument to control the system that we have and to ensure that it's delivering a safe and efficient system for our riders.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We've made changes to our fare policy, which are equitable.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: They're really supporting the growth of our system so that we can allow the regular riders to have access to the

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: same fare as a subway or a bus, introduced and expanded our discount program, and at the same time allowed people who are willing to pay a little bit more to do just that.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So I think that over the last several years, we've focused a lot on fixing and making sure that the system

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: itself is working well and I'm really proud of where we are.

chapters.summary: Wong says fuel is a major cost driver; EDC hedges fuel prices and is hedged through most of the current fiscal year.
chapters.title: Maloney asks about fuel costs and hedging

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: What are some of the largest expenses and how has fuel prices impacted the operational efficiency of the ferry system?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Yeah, fuel is a major cost driver for the system.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: I'm happy to report that because we are able to hedge the pricing on fuels,

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: on fuel in the future, we've done very well with our ability to keep fuel prices in check.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We have seen increases, that is true, but we are not seeing the same kind of increases that are everywhere else because we've been able to hedge in future time.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We are still looking ahead and of course, you know, future cost of fuel is increasing, so that is an area that we're keeping an eye on.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: When would that you expect fuel prices to increase?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We have a continuous hedging program.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We are hedged through most of the current fiscal year.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So we make regular decisions on how to extend that and what price points to do so.

chapters.summary: Wong says Rockaway summer weekends are full; East River capacity expanded by splitting routes; Rockaway Reserve offers paid seat reservations.
chapters.title: Maloney asks which ferry routes are near capacity

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Which routes are operating near capacity or substantially below capacity and how has ridership changed?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So, you know, because it's all at different times of the year, there's times when there are going to be vessels that are very full.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Going to the Rockaways on a summer weekend, they're going to be full vessels.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: But in general, there's often space for us to get more riders on board.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: It's important for us that in the morning and evening peak,

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: periods.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We have enough capacity to get people to work and to school.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
