utterances.text: We think that that's the most important time that we cannot say, sorry, the vessel is full.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: And that was one of the areas where on the East River, we started to have to do that.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: There were times when people were standing at a landing and it's the morning and they're trying to get to a meeting and they couldn't get on board.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: That to us was a real issue that needed to be addressed.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: And as part of the optimization from last year that we implemented in December, we've actually opened up a tremendous amount of capacity because we now run that as two routes.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: And we've seen tremendous growth, which means there were a lot of people who wanted to ride that route, and now they're able to do so.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: In other places, I had mentioned the Rockaway route, you know, the beach route, which is now extended all the way to the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: You can start in the Bronx and get all the way to the Rockaways.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: It is a long trip.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: But in order to help manage the demand on those places, we also introduced opportunities like Rockaway Reserve, where you can reserve a seat.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: You can, you're allowed to pay more and to have access to a reserved seat, which gives people more confidence about which trips they're going to make.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: But broadly, you know, we have, we continue to have space to grow.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We're excited about that because we want to see more people on the system.

chapters.summary: Wong says the four bills are far from existing service areas; each new route would cost $5-6 million annually for two vessels; detailed analysis is in the vision study.
chapters.title: Maloney asks for cost breakdown of proposed ferry routes

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: You mentioned in your statement that the routes that would, the study would require an additional, eight additional vessels and roughly 25 to 30 million for the expanded routes.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Do you have a breakdown of which of the proposed

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: routes would be more expensive for the city to implement versus others?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Yeah, so in order to respond as part of our process here, just in considering the bills, we did take a sort of high-level assessment.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So I would not describe this as the fine detail if we were doing that.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: That's part of our vision study.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: But we did take a quick look at the distance of some of the sites.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Notably, for the four bills that were presented, they're all quite far away from our existing service area.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: And that is one of the single biggest cost drivers for a service, is how far away is it from where you go already.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So places like Canarsie, City Island, West 125th Street, and Willits Point all exist pretty far away.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: They're not, you know, a stop along the way on an existing route.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: And so each of these, we think, has a net operating cost of between $5 and $6 million a year.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: And that's just to run it with two vessels back and forth.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We did not sort of take it too much further in the analysis where we would say, you know, do you have a spare vessel for it?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Do you want more service?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: This is just the minimum that you need to have a regular service.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So, you know, they have reasonably high costs, and we would want to think about things like that in the context of a larger route.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: You know, we rarely run a point-to-point service, but, you know, to quickly map out some of the costs, that's how we started.

chapters.summary: Wong says New York Waterway operates near West 125th Street; the vision study will explore private operator opportunities without public subsidy.
chapters.title: Maloney asks if other ferry systems operate near proposed sites

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And are there other ferry systems that operate near those sites?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: At West 125th Street,

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: New York Waterway, which is a private operator that does a lot of trans-Hudson service, does operate in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So we think that that, for example, as part of the vision study, we would want to explore, you know, is there an opportunity for them to do so?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: And again, we are trying to be good stewards of public funds.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: If there is a way for a private operator to do this without public subsidy, we think that that's a great opportunity.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: And so we'd love to continue having conversations like that.

chapters.summary: Wong says the Hornblower contract expires in 2028 with two three-year extensions; it is premature to decide on extension or a new RFP.
chapters.title: Maloney asks about ferry contract expiration and extensions

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And when is the current contract up for renegotiation?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Yeah, so NYC Ferry is run through a contract with Hornblower, which is a private company providing the ferry services.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Our current contract has an expiration in 2028, but it also has two three-year extensions that were built in and allow the city with predetermined cost functions, knowing fully what the sort of like future costs are going to be.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Those are all baked into the extension.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So they're non-negotiated extensions that we have available.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And when will EDC decide whether or not they plan to exercise that extension or solicit a new RFP or a new partner?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Yeah, we think it's premature to make decisions today about the future of the system.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We still have two years left on this contract.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So we are paying close attention to it and, of course, at all times keeping a close eye on how the operator is performing.

chapters.summary: Wong lists five KPIs: on-time performance, completed trips, customer satisfaction, tech uptime, and maintenance.
chapters.title: Maloney asks about ferry contract KPIs

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: The current contract has some of the KPIs are on-time performance and customer satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Any other KPIs that you're evaluating the performance of the contract based on?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So there are five KPIs that we have built into the system.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So it's on-time performance, completed trips, customer satisfaction, tech uptime, and maintenance.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So on all five of those, what we had decided when we were building out the system originally was we wanted to have something that's easy to manage and really straightforward.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: And for each of these, we have very clear measurements on what they are going to measure and how they are going to make sure that the system is being operated safely and efficiently.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So, for example, completed trips.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Yes, we are measuring the number of trips in the schedule that the operator is delivering, but there are a lot of things that go into that, right?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Like you need your system to be maintained.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: You need your crew to be available.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: You need fuel in the vessel.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: There's all the things come together at these five KPIs to help us really manage the system well.

chapters.summary: Wong says the contract includes a revenue generation section; EDC gets a share from activations, concessions, and advertising.
chapters.title: Maloney asks if contract incentivizes revenue generation

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And does the contract incentivize for creative ways to reduce the subsidies required by New York City government as part of the contract or reduce the cost of operations?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So as part of the contract we have, and this is new when we re-procured it, was a whole section on revenue generation.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: It allows us to work with the operator to do things.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Perhaps you've seen some of the activations and the fun things that you see on our social media.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Some of the, many of those are paid activations for which EDC gets a slice.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: of that revenue.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So we get things, we get some revenue from the concessions, from advertising, from activations, and things like that.

chapters.summary: Wong says digital screens inside vessels sell ads; exterior advertising is prohibited by zoning; EDC has never advertised private companies on exteriors.
chapters.title: Maloney questions ferry advertising and exterior branding

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: On the side of revenue, does the city currently offer sponsorships on boats?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Advertising?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We have digital screens inside the vessels on which we do sell advertising.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So anyone who's interested is able to purchase advertising much like you would see in the subway.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We are not able to advertise on the outside of vessels.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: That's in violation of a zoning code.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: And it's part of beautification within the harbor and the highways.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So we don't have advertising on the outside of vessels.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: That said, the activations that we do inside also extend beyond just the screens.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So sometimes we'll have characters on board, we'll have people doing activations, giveaways for riders.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: In fact, recently with one brand, they were actually paying for people to have free rides.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So throughout the month of October, on each week there was a different route that had a free ride on a Thursday.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So people could just ride for free.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So there are different ways that we work with companies to try to provide something for them.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: They're trying to get their name out, but also something for our riders.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Some private operators do advertise on the exterior, estimating about $20,000 per month per boat.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: advertising revenue, are they not subject to the same zoning constraint that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: I can't really speak to other operators.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: I do know that within New York's waters, there are strict zoning rules about what can be displayed on the exterior of vessels, which doesn't include advertising.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And has EDC done advertising in the past?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I believe they did a few years ago, exterior advertising.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We've never advertised for private companies.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We've had activations.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: There was one for Pride, which was more decorative.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: And then we had one for the World Cup, which was celebrating the various boroughs that we have.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Beyond that, we don't put brands on the outside, the exteriors of vessels.

chapters.summary: Wong says the system was built 100% accessible with bow loaders and wheelchair spaces; EDC is exploring striping, accessible ticket machines, and additional tie-downs.
chapters.title: Maloney asks about accessibility investments on NYC Ferry

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I wanted to also ask about accessibility on the New York City Ferry systems and what investments you've been making there.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Yeah, accessibility is incredibly important to NYC Ferry.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We built the system from the ground up trying to build a fully 100% accessible system.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: And we have all of our landings, every new landing that we've built has automatic bow loaders to ensure that there's level boarding across the system.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: There's all of our vessels have spaces for people using wheelchairs, walkers, or scooters.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: You know, we have all the certainly necessary pieces for that, but we're also trying to do more.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Recently, we've been exploring new striping plans on our landings to improve the visual lines.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: on the exterior of landing so that people with visual disabilities know where the edge is and where to be.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We're also procuring new ticketing machines, which are designed to be more accessible than the ones that we have today.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: And finally, we've been approached in the past at looking at additional ways to improve the accessible spaces on board vessels with additional tie down points.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: And that's something we are looking into.

chapters.summary: Wong says EDC considers ridership potential, alternatives, upland access, water depth, flow, tunnels, capital and operating costs, and economic justice indicators.
chapters.title: Maloney asks how EDC evaluates new ferry routes

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And one final question before I pass to the majority leader.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: How, when you're evaluating new ferry routes and landings, how do you decide what is viable?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: How do you consider what would be a good new route?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And what criteria can you share with the public so that the communities that are requesting services have a better understanding into how these decisions are made?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: There's a lot that go into it, of course.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: You know, when we're looking at new services, a couple of different things that come to mind.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So as a starting point, ridership potential is one of the most important things.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Anything we build, we want it to be useful.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We want it to be delivering for New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We want people to use it.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: And it's not to say that we're only looking at the highest ridership places.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: You know, you might have slightly lower but very impactful ridership.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So we take a look at all the impacts related to who would ride, what they would get out of it.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Is a ferry, for example, faster than the train in some places?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: The geography of certain bays and areas in New York mean that you might have to go around a pretty large landmass.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So when we look at ridership, we are thinking about what people's alternatives are.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: In terms of actual sites, there's a lot that we think about on both the upland and the in-water side.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: From an upland perspective, we want sites that are very accessible to neighborhoods or commercial areas, right?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We don't want it to be behind a highway.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We don't want it to be through a stark walking corridor that people are not comfortable with.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: If those conditions exist, we need to figure out ways to improve those, which does often...

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: come with cost, but those are important parts so that people would be comfortable using some of these.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: On the water side, while starting out in this, I was not as oriented towards maritime, and in Google Maps you see anywhere that's blue is a place you can put a ferry, but in fact the depth of the water, the direction of the water flow,

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: the nearby operations, if there are in-water existing recreational users, there's a lot of different pieces that we check.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Are there subway tunnels underneath?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Like, you know, all the pieces that we want to think about, which are really critical to the construction.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: All of these kind of drive towards capital and operating costs that we look at.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: But I really also want to make sure that we're talking about the economic justice indicators that we are focused on, especially as part of the vision.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: In the vision, we're looking at things like income, demographics, existing access to jobs, and making sure that we are evaluating, as I said, not only high ridership places, but impactful ridership.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: And so a lot of that is part of it.

chapters.summary: Wong says transit deserts are real; ferry can help if faster than alternatives; EDC works with MTA to extend bus routes to landings.
chapters.title: Maloney asks about transit deserts and ground connections

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Do you consider whether or not a location is in a transit desert, if there are alternate options like access to the subway?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And then how do you think about ground transit to match with ferry routes?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: I think that, you know,

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Transit deserts are real.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Not every place has a subway that goes right to it.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: And we think that that's an important thing to be thinking about.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: If places don't have great transit, is ferry a good alternative?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Well, sometimes it is if there's a straight shot over the

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: water and all the conditions we talked about mean that you can take a ferry much faster than you might be able to take a subway or the bus to the subway, that's an important consideration.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Alternatively, even if an area doesn't have great access to transit, sometimes a ferry is not necessarily faster, and we also want to be thoughtful about those pieces.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: In terms of ground transportation, everywhere that we've built ferry landings or have ferry landings, we've worked with MTA to extend bus routes, mainly is probably the main way that we try to better connect, just to create some of that area that people can go to.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: But what we often find is that the area we want to put a ferry in, which doesn't have a bus line nearby or a subway, people are willing to go to it because of that, and that's what we're trying to solve for.

chapters.summary: Abreu notes Intro 1022 requires a terminal by 2028; Wong says EDC studied West 125th in 2018 and earlier, with subway competition as a challenge.
chapters.title: Abreu asks if EDC evaluated West 125th Street ferry

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Now Council Member Abreu, Majority Leader Abreu.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Like technology, we've been joined by Council Member Silvina Brooks-Powers.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And Council Member Aviles.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Well, thank you so much to the administration for coming to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Intro number 1022, sponsored by myself, would require ferry service to a terminal at or near West 125th Street on the Hudson River by January 1st, 2028.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: EDC already manages the West Harlem Pier through Dock NYC.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: But its planned 125th Street landing is in East Harlem.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: My question is, had EDC evaluated West 125th Street as a New York City?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: I'm happy to speak to you again.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We've had some prior conversations about this, and I think it's an ongoing conversation that we really value because the advocacy is important for ferry sites.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We have looked at West 125th Street in prior studies.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: You have?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: In like the 2018 study, yes.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: And then even prior to that, when the system was first being built.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: And some of the challenges that were identified at the time mainly had to do with competition with the subway to get to, you know, is it a faster mode given some of the subway access?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: You know, those are studies of the past.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: I want to be clear that as we are looking through the vision study this time, what we are trying to do is say, let's not look only at, you know, can NYC ferry the subsidized city system provide access to this neighborhood?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Are there other ways that we can activate it?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: And so one of the things we are looking at, particularly at West 125th, is whether or not there are private entities that, you know, might be better suited because they are already operating in the area.

chapters.summary: Wong estimates $26 million for two 150-passenger vessels and $1 million for landing upgrades; more detail will come in the vision study.
chapters.title: Abreu asks about capital costs for West 125th Street ferry

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: In the 2018-2019 Ferry Expansion Feasibility Study, EDC estimated that the West 125th Street site would require $8 million in capital funding to accommodate a passenger ferry and make the site viable.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What is EDC's current estimate for any improvements to ferry infrastructure that would be required at the West Harlem Piers?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So when we did an initial estimate, and again, we are doing more detailed work through the vision study, but in an effort to provide some early information related to the bills, we did put some information together.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: At West 125th Street, we are adding to our costs about $26 million for the cost of two 150 passenger vessels.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So because West 125th Street is a little more than four miles outside of our existing service area, in order to reach it, you need to have actually more vessels on the routes that we operate than we have today.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So that would be the cost for two vessels, you said?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And then in terms of the actual...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: location, the dock, the landings.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Are there any capital estimates you have for that that you would need?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We added a million dollars to our first cut estimate here.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: A million?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Yes, because we looked at it and there is a barge there that is technically usable by our ferry vessels.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: What we do want to make sure is that if we're providing regular ferry service anywhere, that it has the right kind of upgrades to be resilient and standardized for the system.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: That was a very preliminary number, but we would take another look at that for permanent service.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And of course, I hope that EDC sees me as a partner here in terms of getting, if there's funding necessary.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: capital funding necessary for the docs themselves, I mean, for any additional capital expenditures, let me know.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: If there's something that you need, let me know because I'll make it a priority.

chapters.summary: Fredrickson says West Harlem Piers is in the public piers program; operators apply through DOC NYC; EDC will get back on usage specifics.
chapters.title: Abreu asks about current boat service at West Harlem Piers

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilman.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How did EDC make the determination of what kind of boat service to allow at the West Harlem piers?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: The existing facility is managed by DOC NYC, so I'll turn to Anton to speak to that.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So West Harlem Piers is part of the public piers program, and there are vessels who are interested in berthing there or landing there can apply through DOC NYC and get a below market rate there.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What kind of boat service is currently allowed at the West Harlem piers and approximately how many boats per day use the piers and approximately how many passengers per year are using the pier?

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: I'd have to get back to you on the specifics on usage there.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Please get us those specifics.

chapters.summary: Abreu says the community wants ferry service; Wong says the vision study will explore alternative service models, including private operators.
chapters.title: Abreu presses EDC on likelihood of West 125th ferry service

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: You mentioned in your testimony that

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: you're looking potentially at private operators at the site.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We just want ferry service there.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And I have made this very, very clear in conversations in private, obviously now in public, that that's something that the community in West Harlem has been asking for for a very long time.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I mean, what's the likelihood that we're going to get ferry service there?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: I think that the goal of our vision study is to expand the way we're thinking about ferries much broader than what we have in the past.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: In the past, we're

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We've looked at what is only NYC ferry.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Full-time, seven-day-a-week, every single day of the year, commuter service at all times.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: And that has created certain constraints because it comes with such a high price tag.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: One of the ways that we're approaching the vision study is exactly as you'd mentioned, to look at some of those alternative service models.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We haven't finished the work.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: I think that we'd like to spend some more time as we go through this to understand, you know, with the routes that are operating nearby, does it make sense for a private operator?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Is that a conversation we can have with them to help see what they would need?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: You know, those are the kind of things that we're going to explore as part of the study.

chapters.summary: Wong says there is no federal land ownership issue and an existing landing makes it easier, but it is premature to prejudge the vision study.
chapters.title: Abreu asks if West 125th is ripe for ferry service

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I don't want to get ahead of the study results, but are you optimistic of something happening on West 125th Street?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: You know, in your testimony, you mentioned that there were some jurisdictional issues with respect to some of those sites.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We don't have those jurisdictional issues along West 125th Street.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: There's not a federal land ownership piece.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So given that, I mean, doesn't that make it more ripe for a place for ferry service?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: I think what I would say is that because there's an existing landing there, I'm certainly not saying that you cannot operate a ferry.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: You can technically operate a ferry to the site.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: I think that when we go through the vision study, what we're really trying to do is make sure that not only from the capital side, but from an operating cost perspective and understanding,

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: you know, how do these things

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: all fit together.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: I think it's premature right now to sort of prejudge what the outcome of that vision study is going to be, but there is definitely a landing there which makes it a little bit easier when you're talking about new services.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And I'm sure Councilmember De La Rosa also has a lot to add shortly on a ferry service for the north to La Marina and also Althea in the West Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We put out an op-ed this morning calling for

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: more interconnectedness along our waters or waterways uptown in the West Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And we hope that in the study that the EDC takes those requests very, very seriously.

chapters.summary: Regan says DOT licenses commuter ferry operators; EDC manages the NYC Ferry contract separately; licensing oversight is DOT.
chapters.title: Abreu asks DOT about private ferry licensing and coordination

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I have some questions for the Department of Transportation while I'm at it.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: DOT operates the Staten Island Ferry and requires any operator seeking landing access at EDC-managed ferry facilities to first obtain a DOT private ferry operator license.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Can you explain which aspects of passenger transportation on the city's waterways are controlled by DOT?

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: So it is...

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: Commuter ferries is really what our licenses focus on.

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: So we issue licenses to private ferry operators who wish to conduct commuter ferry services in New York City waters.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How do DOT and EDC coordinate on the licensing and oversight of private ferry operators?

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: Licensing oversight is really in New York City DOT.

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: EDC manages the NYC ferry contract separately.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I like your responsiveness to questions.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: You're like, you answer, you can be moving.

chapters.summary: Regan says resources are currently sufficient; challenges include staffing licensed mariners and NYPD coverage; service runs on a mandated schedule.
chapters.title: Abreu asks about Staten Island Ferry resources and challenges

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Unlike New York City Ferry, the Staten Island Ferry,

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: is operated directly by DOT, which you could call the city's longest running fast and free public transit service.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Does the Staten Island Ferry currently have enough resources to meet the demands on the system?

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: Currently, yes.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What are the primary challenges facing the Staten Island Ferry?

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: Staffing is always an issue.

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: You know, licensed mariners filling civil service titles.

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: And also NYPD coverage is an issue on the Staten Island Ferry.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How often does DOT evaluate Staten Island Ferry Service to identify needed operational or policy changes?

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: Well, Staten Island Ferry Service runs on a mandated schedule under the city's administrative code.

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: So we just follow Coast Guard regulations and we follow the mandated schedule and do it as safe an operation as we can.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And the frequency...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Actually, just disregard that.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'll move on to the next question.

chapters.summary: Regan says $1 million in federal funding was fully used for camera systems at Whitehall; DOT will apply for future port security grants.
chapters.title: Abreu asks about Staten Island Ferry security upgrades

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: In 2024, DOT secured $1 million in federal funding to upgrade outdated security systems at Staten Island ferry terminals.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How much of that funding has been used?

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: All of it.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Where have the upgrades been made?

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: To the camera systems.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Any specific locations?

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: 2024, I believe, was the Whitehall Ferry Terminal.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What impacts have you seen as a result of these upgrades?

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: Improved video surveillance, which also obviously helps 24-7 operations with the terminals.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Is there a, will the admin be seeking additional funding for these kind of upgrades?

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: As long as the federal government is issuing port security grant funding, we will always try to apply for any applications that are available at the moment.

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: Currently, no.

chapters.summary: Regan says he will get back on procurement or operational issues since the 2025 transition to renewable diesel.
chapters.title: Abreu asks about Staten Island Ferry renewable diesel transition

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: In the summer of 2025, the city announced that the Staten Island Ferry had transitioned to 100% renewable diesel fuel.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Have there been any issues related to procurement or operations in the year since that transition?

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: I'll have to get back to you with that information.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Please do.

chapters.summary: Fredrickson says it is a joint program with an annual industry day and pilot collaboration; Regan says DOT modified the private ferry license for micro freight.
chapters.title: Abreu asks about DOT-EDC Blue Highways partnership

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: In October 2025, DOT and EDC jointly published a Blue Highways Action Plan for developing a cleaner, safer, and more resilient freight system in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How does the partnership between DOT and EDC work with regard to Blue Highways?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What is the division of responsibility and authority between the two agencies?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: You want to start on Blue Highways?

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: Sure, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So it's a joint program between DOT and EDC, and the Blue Highways Action Plan was a document that we collaborated on together.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: We also co-host a Blue Highways Industry Day every year.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: We engage with private operators throughout the ecosystem.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: And we also look at pilots together.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So we collaborated on a pilot blue highway service for a couple months between the Brooklyn Marine Terminal and Pier 79.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So I know it's an ongoing collaborative relationship.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And what would you say is the division of responsibility and authority between the two agencies?

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: So for the DOTs supporting Blue Highways throughout the city, but we were really looking at trying to leverage the existing ferry routes for Blue Highways operations.

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: So to that end, we modified the private ferry operator license to allow for some Blue Highways pilots and work at our ferry landings.

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: Otherwise, we're supporting EDC and the EDC.

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: endeavor of trying to move as much freight off the roadways and onto the waterways.

chapters.summary: Fredrickson says downtown Skyport construction starts soon for Blue Highways berthing; Regan says pilots tested Pier 79 and East 34th Street dockings.
chapters.title: Abreu asks about Blue Highways progress and micro freight

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What progress has the city made toward the goals in the action plan?

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So we're not only exploring and evaluating sites, we're actually advancing them further.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So one example is the downtown Skyport, formerly known as the downtown Manhattan heliport.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: As part of that re-procurement, we added a requirement to build out a Blue Highways birthing infrastructure, and we are

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: in a couple weeks beginning construction there.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So some more to come on that front, and that landing will open by the end of next year.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So this is like real construction beginning to take place on a key node to lower Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: And we're doing this across the city as well.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: As part of the action plan, DOT committed to test the feasibility of using DOT ferry landings to receive micro freight.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What steps has the OC taken to move this proposal forward?

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: So in conjunction with EDC, we did run a test pilot to Pier 79, which is a New York City DOT-owned ferry landing.

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: We also have done some test.

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: Blue highways dockings at the East 34th Street ferry landing to see the feasibility of using that landing for operations.

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: And then, like I said, we did modify our private ferry operator license to give existing operators the opportunity to move micro freight on their ferry boats, obviously within Coast Guard regulation.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Banks describes his district as an affordable housing hub and transit desert; Wong says there have been no substantive talks with state parks but will follow up.
chapters.title: Banks asks about ferry at Shirley Chisholm Park and state talks

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Council Member Banks?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't give you a heads up.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: That was coming.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: You ready?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you, Chiz.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: First of all, I just want to say that my district is a unique district.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: We are actually, a portion of the district has created probably the largest amount of affordable housing throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And then the other portion, which is the East Flatbush, is part of the bottom 12.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And when we're talking about the expansion of transportation, we want, obviously, we want to look at every, you know, option.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And we also know that we have the Shirley Chisholm Park, which is obviously a space that is heavily utilized.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Has there been any talks with the state?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: As you do know, that is a state park to possibly consider there for possibly having it be a ferry.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks

chapters.summary: Wong says the vision study looks beyond NYC Ferry to alternative operators, funding models, and seasonal or weekend service.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: I think NYC Ferry, which did have a large growth spread and has come online over the last 10 years, is one kind of ferry service.

chapters.summary: Wong says the study will examine ridership, demographics, transit access, commercial corridors, site suitability, and economic impact.

utterances.speaker: James Wong

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So we'll look at a lot of different things like that.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Are you also considering the potential impact that ferry service could have on the local economy?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Yes, we take a look at the land uses nearby and like I was saying, are there commercial corridors and things like that that we can identify as hotspots where if you have ferry service, could this be supportive?

chapters.summary: Wong says the study considers congestion and whether ferry would exacerbate traffic; landings are built resilient to sea level rise but not full resiliency projects.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about City Island traffic and environmental risks

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And City Island, as my colleague mentioned, has one road in and one road out.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: City Island, as my colleague mentioned, has one road in and one road out, which leads to serious congestion along the island that affects cars, buses, emergency vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Will traffic congestion be taken into consideration in the study?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Can EDC estimate a decrease in car traffic that a ferry could potentially lead to?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Looking at existing transportation is an important part of looking at ferry opportunities.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: As you pointed out, because it has a pretty congested single road down the middle for much of City Island, that is one of the things we consider, and whether or not bringing a ferry landing would in fact exacerbate traffic problems if people are coming in to use it from beyond City Island.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So, you know, these are the kind of things we think about when we're exploring the ideas.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: The coastal areas of the East Bronx, including City Island, have also had serious pollution challenges and flood risks.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: DLT and DDC are looking at many resilience and mitigation plans in the area, but there's still a lot of work to be done.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol

utterances.text: account climate change risks, changes to water level and shorelines, you know, garbage and pollutants spilling into East Chester Bay.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So how will, you know, will your study take a look at the environmental factors?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: As a general matter, when we're looking at specific sites, if we're considering a specific area, then we are considering whether or not it has the existing upland infrastructure to handle it.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: NYC Ferry in the past, and the way we've approached these, has not been to sort of bite off an entire resiliency project, but rather to see are there adequate facilities nearby at which we can site a ferry landing.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Ferry landings are, by their nature, able to handle some amount of sea level rise, but we make sure that the piles are high enough, that the landings are built in a resilient way, that the slope of the gangways are not going to be in excess.

utterances.speaker: James Wong

utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: I have had in conversations I've had with residents have been that they're excited about, you know, we're excited about the Ferry Point landing, are utilizing the Ferry Point Park landing.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Because there's a huge parking lot there, have the ability to park there.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: So I just want to raise in that response of like the potentiality of congestion.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I think we all know from seeing ferry landings appear throughout the city of New York, there's always about a quarter of excitement.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And then it kind of swells out.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: We experienced that in Soundview where we had some parking mishaps and things like that because we don't have a parking lot.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I think what's afforded at the ferry point landing is that there is a parking lot.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: People that need to drive to a ferry landing have typically already evaded going to Soundview and go right there to leave their vehicle.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And I personally do not think that that would be something that would happen.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: On City Island too frequently.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Have you folks thought through in the optimization plan, just to what Councilmember De La Rosa was saying, looking at the landing not just for the

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: best case scenario in ridership, but also looking at the economic impacts that

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: that could be the best case scenario for communities that would result in getting a ferry landing.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: As part of the vision study, we're trying to bring an economic justice lens to this, which looks beyond just, you know, are there places with the highest ridership and, you know, how do we build more of those?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: If that were the lens, the only things that would get built are places, you know, Dumbo has some of our highest ridership, but that's not what we're trying to do.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We're trying to build out, or we're trying to consider whether or not we should grow, and if we are, how to do that in the most impactful ways.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Impact to us means taking a look at where people live, what the demographics are, what their economic opportunities are, and whether ferry could help improve those.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So those are some of the ways that we're looking at it.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Would you folks consider a high percentage of commercial corridor that's vacant a place to look at boosting the local economy?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: I think that, you know, it is certainly an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: It also creates risk, you know, at the same time.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: You know, is this a place that people are coming to?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: I think that very often does create ways for people to enter into communities and can really support them.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: A good example that we've seen recently in Red Hook, and there's been some good coverage over the summer of people who are coming in and exploring and finding places.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: To the extent you like seeing lots of people coming into a community to shop and do business there on weekends, we see a lot of that.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: And so, you know, we see the power of NYC Ferry, and I want to explore that more.

chapters.summary: Farias asks how seasonal pilots inform long-term landings; Wong says Rockaway Rocket continues and the optimization added a year-round one-seat ride.
chapters.title: Farias asks about Rockaway Rocket pilot and comprehensive plan

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And just in my last minute of questioning that I have,

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: What was looked at for the Rockaway Rocket pilot opportunity, and how is...

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: that if at all being included in looking at the larger comprehensive plan on landings and where there's short-term seasonal opportunity that can then maybe over time, like we've seen with the Rockaway rocket,

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: transition into a long-term standing ferry landing.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Yeah, the Rockaway Rocket was a pilot that we continue to operate because we continue to see demand for a very limited number of trips from places in Queens and its Long Island City and Greenpoint.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: And that provides some direct access to the Rockaways, whereas the route that we actually extended through the optimization allowed for regular full-time service all year round.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So that if you're in the Bronx or the Upper East Side, you can have a one-seat ride all the way to the Rockaways, and that's year-round.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So it shows us that people are trying to go to the Rockaways, and it gives us opportunities to serve them in different ways.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I guess just in the entrance of time that...

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I'm more so looking at all of the bills that are in front of you folks over many years.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: We've been through this our fifth year together on this committee, looking at the different areas in the city of New York where people see landings as desirable, despite feasibility or not.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: New Yorkers are asking for their neighborhoods on the waterfront to be seen as a place where they can either have another commuting option, a commercial booster,

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: seasonal commercial booster.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I'm just wondering when we're looking at our long-term comprehensive plan on landings in priority order or

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: you know, in the order of interest, whether it's economic or transportation justice related or not, how are we ensuring that we're using multiple options on getting New Yorkers accessibility throughout the city of New York?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: I think the vision plan genuinely is the way that we're going to achieve the exact goal that you're talking about, which is to say, let's not just look at it one way.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Let's not just look at the previous studies we've done before and try and take a more open approach to these.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So that's what we're working on and plan to deliver by next summer.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: And we'll have a lot more to say as we go through that process.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: One last question, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Are we going to stay on time since we're late already on this plan?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Are we going to be on time for 2027 since the plan's already late?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: That is our intention to deliver this by summer.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: All right, I'm going to hold you to it.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs.

chapters.summary: Aviles says EDC should track economic impacts; Wong cites press coverage but no on-the-ground data; Aviles notes visitors often take cabs away.
chapters.title: Aviles asks who tracks economic impact of ferry in Red Hook

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Aviles, followed by Wong.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: about the next hearing I have to be at a couple minutes.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: So I'd like to follow up on who's collecting data on the economic impact of the ferry and Red Hook?

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Since you referenced Red Hook and seeing so much benefit, who's collecting that data?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We don't have on the ground data.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: What I was referring to, there was press coverage earlier this summer that just talked about the sort of waves of people that are coming into the community throughout the summer.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Yeah, lots of people coming in.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Yeah, it would be great.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: I mean, this is a conversation, obviously.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: We have been trying very hard to actually get

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: EDC to connect with the local community, to engage in full comprehensive work to connect the assets of the local community so that benefits stay.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
