chapters.summary: Aviles asks about the BMT-Pier 79 pilot; Regan says Dutch X moved micro freight but had logistical issues; Aviles says the pilot is minuscule for freight needs.
chapters.title: Aviles questions scale of Blue Highways pilot

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Like many communities in the city, I mean, I'd like to talk specifically about the Blue Highway.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: You mentioned in your testimony an example, and I'm so just, can you tell us more specifically

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: how you noted a pilot between BMT and Pier 79.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Can you be more specific about the scale and scope of that pilot and how we have used our ferry system, not just Staten Island Ferry, but how have we utilized the ferry system

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: to advance blue highways?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Yeah, you want to start?

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: Are we afternoon yet?

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: Almost afternoon.

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: Who knows?

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: Almost afternoon.

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: So for NYC DOT ferries, I had mentioned earlier, we modified our private ferry operator license so that existing operators could move micro freight on existing ferry routes.

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: That was very important to us.

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: We wanted to leverage the existing routes to try to get some of the freight off the highways and onto the waterfront, onto the vessels.

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: So, so far we have had one pilot go to Pier 79 and that was a company called Dutch X who was moving micro freight from Brooklyn to the west side of Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: That was very successful, but they ran into some logistical issues on the Dutch X side.

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: So much of the ferry side.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Yeah, Dutchess has gone from Red Hook, right?

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: They were on the water, Red Hook.

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: I'm not sure where they are.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Yeah, they moved on.

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: Yeah, they're done.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: They've left Pier 11, and they're looking for new space along the waterfront.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Okay, so how much freight was moved during that pilot?

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: I'd have to get back to you with that.

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: I don't have it today.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: I think, you know, I...

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Pilots are important, right, to obviously proof of concept, but it really does seem like this pilot is minuscule for the scale and scope of our commitment to moving freight, particularly from a community that is deluge with trucks,

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: has an abundance of waterfront, and nothing is getting moved by the water.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: So I guess my message in short is,

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: We want to see a much more aggressive position to using our current infrastructure, not just the things we need to build out.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: I'm glad the sky port is eventually going to get there.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: But we do have, we're moving vessels throughout the city, and how we are not leveraging that in a more aggressive way is really surprising to me.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: So I don't know if you want to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: No, I mean, we certainly share the opportunity that the waterways offer in terms of freight.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: I think the counterbalance may be just on the other end of that node for that pilot, and that's why we're starting a crawl-walk.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: Kind of run approach is we want to make sure that we're integrating these e-quads or e-bikes with, you know, integrating it carefully with the surrounding streetscape on the other end of the node.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So it's always a balance.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: And that's why we're looking at separate or in addition to the ferry landings are can we have dedicated landings for blue highways where you don't have necessarily that conflict or you can design it even better.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So that's, you know, you mentioned downtown Skyport.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: We're very excited to bring that one online by the end of next year.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: And we look forward to activating other nodes along the waterfront specific to Blue Highway's shipment.

chapters.summary: Aviles asks if EDC has a full assessment of assets and will make it public; Fredrickson says he will get specifics and notes landings are incremental new infrastructure.
chapters.title: Aviles asks for public assessment of pier and landing repair

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: So we know that the state of repair of much of this infrastructure is not good.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Do you have a full assessment of what each of these either landings or the state of peer repair is for all of the assets within EDC portfolio?

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: And will you make that public?

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: Yeah, I can get back to you with specifics on numbers.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: I will say that.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: The landings that we're looking at are typically incremental or net new, so we're building them in addition to the existing waterfront that we already maintain, whether it be for public waterfront access or industrial uses or

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: ferry landing.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So it's new infrastructure that we're adding to the existing waterfront.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Wong asks if ferries communicate with seaplanes; James Wong says ferry captains use a public channel; Fredrickson says seaplanes radio before landing and coordinate with LaGuardia tower.
chapters.title: Phil Wong asks about ferry-seaplane communication

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Councilmember Wong, followed by Brooks Powers.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: First question is regarding the seaplane taking off and landings.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I had a friend that was stuck in Newark Airport.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: when the bakery truck, when the plane trying to land and struck a lamppost, and then the bakery truck, and then the airport was closed.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: My question is, do your ferries communicate with seaplanes whenever they take off and land, or there is no communication and they play by ear?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Can you please answer that?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Our ferry captains are on a public channel that seaplanes are able to access as well.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: But do they listen to?

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: Yeah, they typically radio in before landing.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So they're coordinated both with the activity on the water as well as with Tower LaGuardia on the airspace side.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yeah, because based upon the photos here, you know, then they can get crowded pretty easily during the summer months.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And if there's no adequate communication, potentially these are accidents waiting to happen.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So communication is certainly one part of that.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: Ensuring safe landings on the waterfront.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: There's also pilot discretion to find navigable water so they can do a turnaround if there isn't a patch of water to land safely.

chapters.summary: Wong asks about the $8.79 subsidy and flat fare; James Wong says it is a system-wide average and same fare policy as the subway; EDC offers a $15 two-day tourist pass.
chapters.title: Phil Wong questions subsidies and tourist pricing

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: My second question is regarding the subsidies.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: In the statement here, you said that in fiscal FY26,

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: The subsidy per ride is $8.79.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So we have a situation here that the more...

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: services we expand, the more subsidies the city has to provide.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So my question to you is that obviously you want to close or lower this subsidy.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And to do that, you have to look at the cost per ride.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I mean, the cost per ride, say, from Lower Manhattan to Long Island City is very different from Lower Manhattan to, say, to the Far Rockaways.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: But right now you have a fixed cost per ride.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yeah, cost the same.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: What we report out and talk about is that $8.79 is a system-wide average.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: But yes, there are different cost functions, as you have pointed out.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Going to some place that is further away does take more fuel, it takes more time.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So there are higher costs associated with places that are further from the core.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Have you considered...

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Pricing them accordingly because at the rate these ferries expand, you have to start looking at cost savings.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And one way to do that is look at the prices you're charging, or perhaps you can offer other packages.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I know tourists that are taking the ferry, they're rather than paying so much more

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: to Circle Line or to Liberty Cruises, they'll rather take NYC Ferry because they can, oh, see the Statue of Liberty, Verrazano Bridge, you know.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So this is something I think you should look into, sell packages to tourists and price accordingly per trip.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: rather than a flat fee because I see that you do not support these bills that's introduced by the city council because of the division study.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: But clearly cost is a big issue because you have capital costs and you have

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: construction costs, you know, and other costs related on expanding the ferry services.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So this is something, are you looking into that, doing some price changes per trip or selling packages?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Yeah, no, thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: I guess as a starting point, as a matter of policy, not unlike the subway, we do charge the same price across the city.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So we don't want to penalize people who live further away with a higher price point.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: But what we do have is a fare structure that does allow us to do exactly what you're talking about, which is to have lower prices for people who are frequent riders and higher prices for someone who's riding just for fun.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: If you are just riding and you only need to ride once, it might behoove you to pay the $5, the higher fare, which we just increased yesterday, actually, from $4.50 to $5.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So it's a higher price if you're riding once in a while and you don't want the package.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Finally, we also have implemented, which is relatively new and targeted more towards tourists, is the $15 two-day pass.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So we invite people who are visiting to come use NYC Ferry and pay $15 for an unlimited number of rides over the course of two days.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We see that as a way to really target tourists.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We are actually advertising and selling those through some of the online vendors as well to get the word out so that we could get people who are willing to pay more onto the system.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So as a tourist, where do they get these two-day passes?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: You can buy them through the app at ticket vending machines or more recently through two.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: They're either on or they're going to be available on Viator and Get Your Guide.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers notes EDC previously said expansion was not viable due to the A-Train bridge; Wong says the vision study looks at smaller vessels inside Jamaica Bay.
chapters.title: Brooks-Powers asks about Eastern Rockaways ferry access

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Councilor Brooks-Powers.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs, and it's good to see you all here today, EDC, with new leadership and folks there.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I'm hoping that there'll be some exciting news as it pertains to the ferry expansion.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So in 2024, EDC told this council that expanding ferry service further into the Rockaways was not viable, mostly because ferries can't fit under the A-Train bridge.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Since then, the Eastern Rockaways have continued to grow, and EDC has redesigned the whole ferry network.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Has EDC taken a new look at the Eastern Rockaways?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So we are looking at it as part of the vision study, and we're looking at it with a broader set of parameters than we have in the past.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: You're absolutely right that our vessels cannot fit under the A-Train bridge, the vessels that we have, which go out to the rockerways, which have to be large enough to get out there safely and carry the passengers.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: So while our existing fleet does not get under that bridge, by looking at this through the vision, we're trying to see are there other ways that we can connect neighborhoods to their waterfronts.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: And so maybe there are smaller vessels.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Maybe they only stay inside Jamaica Bay.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Maybe they connect to Beach 108th Street for continuing service.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We're trying to map out all the different opportunities and what they might cost and how feasible they are.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I really appreciate hearing that.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I will say after four years of hearing no, just hearing the openness is definitely welcome.

chapters.summary: Wong says the one-seat ride benefits Rockaway riders and Bronx or Upper East Side riders; 9% of summer ridership used new connections.
chapters.title: Brooks-Powers asks how combined Soundview-Rockaway route works

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: In terms of Rockway Riders, EDC's own optimization plan found the Rockways have limited access to Midtown.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Following that plan, reconfigurations were made combining the Soundview and Rockway routes to provide additional one-seat connection to Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: How has the new combined route worked for Rockway rides?

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: We see it as beneficial because people are able to have that one-seat ride, so now if you start in the Rockaways, you do not need to transfer, and the people who were switching vessels at Pier 11 and waiting and sometimes missing a vessel no longer have to do that.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: It also allows people to make further trips that are going further north.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: From the north for folks in the Bronx, it gives them a way to get into the Rockaways.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: It is a long trip, but if you are on the Upper East Side or in the Bronx and you want to visit the Rockaways,

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: Rockaways, these provide new opportunities.

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: I don't have the ridership numbers in front of me, but I will say that what we have seen as part of our summer evaluation is that almost 9% of the trips that were taken on NYC Ferry over the summer,

utterances.speaker: James Wong
utterances.text: or since between May and mid-September, were trips that you could not make in the past.

utterances.speaker: James Wong

utterances.text: We look to partner with council members and community groups.

utterances.text: operator to try and get people to know about NYC Ferry and the discount program.

chapters.summary: Fredrickson says the seaplane base is part of the DOC NYC public piers program; the operator ensures licenses and SOPs; EDC oversees the contract.
chapters.title: Maloney asks who oversees Skyport seaplane base

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I have a second round of questions focused on seaplanes.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I want to get into the oversight and accountability aspects, specifically who at EDC is responsible for overseeing the Skyport Marina seaplane dock on the city's behalf.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So the seaplane base is part of the city's public peers program called DocNYC.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So it's that same operator that also manages and ensures that all the necessary licenses and checks are in place for each of the seaplane operators.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: There's also a standard operating procedure that they publish that all seaplane users, and in addition to all Coast Guard regs and FAA regs, they follow the protocols or the SOP of the third-party seaplane base operator.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So what does EDC itself have direct oversight over versus delegating to Billy Bay Marina Services or Doc NYC?

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So we oversee that contract.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So we have a

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: oversight over that contract.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: We both competitively procure it and have the ability to reassess at certain periods of time and there's ongoing engagement and checks with them as well.

chapters.summary: Fredrickson says the SOP requires takeoff 1,000 feet from shore; pilots have discretion for weather; DOC NYC monitors and can penalize.
chapters.title: Maloney asks about safety of East River residents and 1000-foot rule

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: There are 250,000 constituents along the East River, many of them my constituents in District 4.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So what is EDC doing to ensure the safety of those New Yorkers who are adjacent to these

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: seaplane operations along the East River.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So as part of the SOP, so first they have to follow all the federal regulations, but in addition, as part of the, we call the airport master record, there are some remarks

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: in there as well as the SOP that DocNYC has.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: And one of them, for example, is that

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: where it's safe that they take off 1,000 feet off of the shore.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So that's one way that we ensure distance and adequate spacing to the coastline.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Who specifically monitors the 1,000 feet from the shore, and what are the consequences when an operator violates that?

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: Yeah, so that is done through DocNYC, but I think there's always opportunities to strengthen kind of tracking of that 1,000-foot offshore rule.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: I will say that there are times when

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: The pilot has the discretion to go closer based on weather or the conditions of the

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: The water.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So it is not like a hard and fixed rule.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: It is a strong recommendation there.

chapters.summary: Fredrickson says DOC NYC contacts operators after the fact; if there is no valid safety reason, penalties are possible; EDC oversees.
chapters.title: Maloney probes enforcement of 1000-foot seaplane rule

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And is that 1,000 feet from the pier or from the shoreline?

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: My understanding based on the reading is from the shoreline.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And what are some of the circumstances where that is shortened and how would you validate that the pilot took off less than a thousand feet in an instance where it was approved?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Who does that approval?

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So it would be after the fact where the Doc NYC would contact the seaplane operator and try to understand it.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: Was there a specific reason for that?

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: And if there wasn't,

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: a valid safety reason, then we would look at potential penalties there.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So DOC NYC is entirely responsible for the enforcement of this 1,000-foot rule?

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: Yes, but through oversight of the EDC as well.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And do you have a sense of how often an operator has violated that rule and what the consequences were?

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: I don't have that information, but I can follow up.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Follow up with that?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Yeah.

chapters.summary: Fredrickson says pilots enter Class Bravo airspace and must turn around; LaGuardia tower steps in; DOC NYC can revoke a license for repeat offenders.
chapters.title: Maloney asks about 59th Street Bridge overflight enforcement

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And similarly, a question on enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Seaplanes are not permitted to fly over the 59th Street Bridge, but who is monitoring that, and what are the consequences for noncompliance with that rule?

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: Yeah, so as you approach 59th Street Bridge, you start entering Class Bravo airspace with LaGuardia, so they will need to turn around to not interfere with the operations of LaGuardia, and that's when the tower steps in.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And so how do they enter the East River Corridor?

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: They're typically coming from the south and turning around, but yeah, depends.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And what sanctions are in place when pilots do not follow the rules?

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: Well, we have the ability through DOCM-RIC to revoke the license if they are found to be a repeated offender of these rules that we put in place.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So we do have that ability to restrict them further.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And how often has that happened?

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: I would have to get back to you.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: I'm not aware of a recent incident.

chapters.summary: Fredrickson says noise abatement is dawn to dusk, nothing overnight; EDC is exploring electric seaplanes and uses ADS-B tracking to monitor flight paths.
chapters.title: Maloney asks about seaplane noise monitoring and abatement

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Another frequent reported issue is noise.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: The New York State Airport Director

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Chapter 3 indicates that New York Skyports has noise abatement in effect for 24 hours, but what noise monitoring is currently being done and what noise abatement is in effect?

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So noise abatement is typically done through the operating hours.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So like, oh no, it's only from dawn to dusk.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So nothing overnight.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: We are also looking at potential new technologies, and this is going to be similar to those who track the helicopter issue, but for electric seaplane operations that are quieter.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So there's a couple of technologies out there, and we're actively engaged with industry to see how we can bring those and safely integrate them into the New York City airspace.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: For both the issue of noise monitoring and tracking where planes are flying or where they're taking off from, what technologies is EDC looking into or is DOC MIC looking into to better enforce

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: these laws?

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: Yeah, so we use ADS-B tracking.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: Which is automatic dependent surveillance, I think that's right, bandwidth.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: And so that's a way, broadcast, sorry, that's what the B stands for, and this is a way to track movements of aircraft to see where they are positioned on the water and whether they are veering off.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So you can set a geographic box to see if they're outside where they're not supposed to be or where they're within the limits.

chapters.summary: Fredrickson says seaplanes date to the 1930s and volumes are 30% below pre-pandemic; EDC regularly reviews their role and will follow up on the Community Board 6 plan.
chapters.title: Maloney asks when EDC last reviewed seaplane operating area

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And how long have seaplanes been operating out of the 23rd Street?

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: Yeah, they have a long history in the East River, so as far back as the 1930s, even prior.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: But this particular seaplane base was built in 1939, I believe, when LaGuardia was made.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: The East River has changed quite substantially from that time, from a more industrial maritime neighborhood to heavily congested residential with waterfront buildings,

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: schools, parks, and the ferry activity that we spent the first half of the hearing talking about.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: When did EDC last evaluate whether or not the operating area is appropriate for seaplanes?

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: Say we're regularly reviewing whether it's a, you know, how seaplanes play a role in the diverse kind of transportation ecosystem of New York.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: I will say that when we compare it to historical volumes, we're still operating below pre-pandemic levels, so approximately 30% below, yeah, pre-pandemics.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Community Board 6 had passed resolutions dating back from 1996 all the way to just last year calling for EDC to develop a plan with community input on community-centered use cases.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: What is the status of that plan?

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: I'd have to get back to you on that specific plan.

chapters.summary: Fredrickson says first responders and federal investigations handle incidents; the July 5 incident paused operations; there were about 1,400-1,500 landings in the six-month season.
chapters.title: Maloney asks about accident accountability and landing frequency

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And when you talk about some of the seaplane operators that use the space,

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Acadian seaplanes, fly the whale, tropic ocean airwines, etc.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Who is accountable if there is an accident or an incident?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And how does Doc NYC know, or EDC, know which company or which person or which plane is responsible?

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: But first, if there's an incident, it's first responders that are onto the scene.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: And then there was coordination with DOC NYC and EDC to make sure that we understand all the facts before we resume operations.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: And so there was a July 5th incident, I think it was mentioned earlier, where we did pause for the remainder of the day to make sure we understood the conditions and then before we resumed activity again.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And the number of landings are more frequent in the summer months, is that right?

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So you see this typically between May and October.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And do you have a sense of the number of landings month by month in that busy period?

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: Yeah, I can give back to you on the exact month by month breakdown, but it was approximately like 1,400, 1,500 this past year.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: Or in 2025, yeah, we're still collecting the final numbers for 2026.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Over that entire period?

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: Over that six-month period.

chapters.summary: Fredrickson says the seaplane base generates about $300,000 annually; DOT says oversight is entirely EDC, FAA, and Coast Guard; registration is with NY State DOT.
chapters.title: Maloney asks about seaplane revenue and DOT registration

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And do you have a sense, or can you share how much revenue the seaplane operations generate annually for the city?

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: Yeah, so it's $300,000 approximately to the dock and rice.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And what are the main...

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: and use cases of these seaplanes.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: It's typically by the seat charters to go out to other waterfront destinations further afield.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So yeah, that's the main activity that we see.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I want to also ask DOT what role you have in overseeing seaplane operations along the East River and which aspects instead fall to the FAA, the Coast Guard, EDC?

utterances.speaker: John Regan
utterances.text: Yeah, it's entirely EDC, FAA, Coast Guard.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Entirely EDC.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I believe that the DOT requires seaplane bases to register every three years.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Is that part of the scope?

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: They're registered with the New York State Department of Transportation.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: With the New York State.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And do you know whether 6 and 7 is registered for the 2026 to 2029 period and which person is listed as the owner or manager?

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: Yes, it would be somebody from DOC NYC.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: I'd have to double check the name on who the name is on that particular record.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: So it's both the state DOT registration, but also with the FAA airport master record as well.

chapters.summary: Maloney notes the vision plan is delayed to summer 2027; EDC cites new administration coordination; funding models are undetermined and EDC is open-minded on the next RFP.
chapters.title: Maloney asks why vision plan is delayed and how it affects budget

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I want to acknowledge that my colleague, Councilmember Sanchez, has joined us.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: On waterfront careers, I wanted to go back to that question from earlier.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: This committee and the council is supportive of the Waterfront Careers Initiative to support CUNY's Maritime Tech Degree Program.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So that is some investment that we are making on that front.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I wanted to push on the vision plan.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: The vision plan is delayed, expected to wrap up in summer 2027.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: That's a full year delayed than the original timeline.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Can you speak to why?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: As we are getting settled in as administration, we are doing ongoing coordination.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: to not only bring folks up to speed, but to make sure that we have a thoughtful approach to the full study.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And will that timeline push up against, say, obviously this is an expensive endeavor.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: We talked about some of that.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: How would that relate to the budget conversations and budget negotiations that we would need to be having?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that as part of the vision study,

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: As I had mentioned, there's kind of a lot of different ways we can think about what kind of funding we're even talking about.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Are we looking for funding at a private operator?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Are we looking at funding through NYC Ferry?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Are we looking for small recreational services?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So I think it's a little early to predetermine what kind of funding we're looking for, we would be looking for, or what would be asked for.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And as you're thinking about the next step in procurement a few years out, is there a world where you'd consider dividing up the system by routes or relying on private operators?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Are you open-minded on how you'll approach the next RFP?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It is right now because we still have two years left.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We haven't made any decisions about the whether to RFP or extend the current operating agreement.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: At whatever time we do put out an RFP, so whether that's, you know, at the end of this term or at the end of

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: one or two of the future terms, we would, of course, take a hard look at the full system to understand how we've been managing it and whether that's the right way to do it.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So we made a lot of major changes to the operating agreement.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: between the first and the second version, I think we now have a much better handle on how to operate it.

chapters.summary: EDC says contracts can be FOILed; some SOPs are security-sensitive; seaplane SOPs can be public; EDC focuses on safety and access and will follow up on metrics.
chapters.title: Maloney asks about public contracts and seaplane KPIs

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: In both the case of NYC Ferry and the case of seaplane operations and party boat operations with DocNYC, there are subcontractor or contracted arrangements.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Those, you mentioned SOPs and guidelines and negotiated terms in these agreements.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Are those agreements made public?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And could we request copies?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Our contract is public.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I mean, it can be foiled to provide access to it.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Sorry, it is, our contracts can be foiled, of course, and can be obtained.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So we can follow up with you on that.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: In terms of specific SOPs, some of them are security sensitive.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Some of them have certain restrictions to them.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So depending on what we're talking about, we can follow up on that.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And on the case of seaplane operations?

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson
utterances.text: Yeah, those are shared with the seaplane operators and can be foiled as well or made public.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And a similar question I asked on the ferry side, but how do you evaluate the KPIs of the seaplane operators?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: What are you measuring?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: In terms of determining or reviewing the appropriateness of a seaplane operator in the area?

utterances.text: So that's one effort we've made in that area.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And to that point, it would be great to follow up with some of the data on the safety metrics that the operators are meeting, as well as

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney

utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Anton Fredrickson

chapters.summary: Aldebol says a ferry could serve commuters, beach, park, and tourism; EDC says the study will assess site suitability and routing, including connections to Soundview and Ferry Point.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about City Island tourism and connections

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I wanted to make sure my colleagues get a chance to ask their second round, starting with Councilmember Aldeball.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Maloney.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So I just want to really want to put the City Island ferry kind of into context.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: You know, a ferry to the City Island area could be sort of multi-purposes.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Similar to existing ferry services in other parts of the city, not only serving commuters and students, but increasing access for non-residents to beach,

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: to the beach, to the park, and other waterfront destinations in the East Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: You know, we have the largest park in New York City, right there across the bridge from City Island.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And, you know, how will that potential be taken into account when you think about ridership?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: It's not just the commuter ridership, but...

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: All of the potential ridership that would be coming on and off the island.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: As part of the vision study, we would look not only at the land uses immediately around any potential landing site, but also for areas where there are willingness to drive further, we would of course look at the surrounding land uses like park uses as well.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And, you know, I do want to...

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I do want to ask again about the potential tourism.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Are you taking into consideration or are you projecting the potential tourism that could come onto the island and to the East Bronx?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We are looking at ways to measure non-commuter rides.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It is sometimes challenging because there are somewhat difficult numbers to make predictions on, so how many people will want to come from a tourism perspective.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: But we are looking throughout the city and the system to find good markers and comparisons that we could use to make those evaluations.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Are you looking at a connection to the Soundview Ferry and Ferry Point as potential ridership?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Yeah, as a starting point, we're looking at specific areas and whether or not they have some of the physical, like the site suitability.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Like, are there sites that you can actually physically put a ferry landing or some other kind of waterfront infrastructure?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Once we go through that, we will, in the future, look at, you know, where would that connect to?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Because, of course, you can't be a ferry in isolation.

chapters.summary: A high school sophomore built a Raspberry Pi system to log helicopter noise and identify aircraft; he shared data with Congressman Latimer and is adapting it for seaplanes near Waterside Plaza.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Our next panel is in person.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: First, Mateo Lallement, Janet Handel, Waterside Tenants Association President,

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Miriam Applebaum, Waterside Plaza resident, Diane Park from Waterside Tenants Association, and Tyler Taba, Waterfront Alliance.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I want to begin with

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Mateo, if you're ready to start, or Janet, whoever's ready to testify.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Mateo, whenever you're ready to begin.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, but can you make sure your microphone is on?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Lawman
utterances.text: Good morning, and thank you for the chance to speak today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Lawman
utterances.text: My name is Mateo Lawman.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Lawman
utterances.text: I'm a high school sophomore from Westchester, and I'm here at the invitation of Janet Handel, president of Waterside Tenants Association.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Lawman
utterances.text: Where I live, helicopters fly over my house as many as 20 times a day, sometimes early in the morning or late at night.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Lawman
utterances.text: They fly low enough that our windows shake.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Lawman
utterances.text: Neighbors who are older can't sleep.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Lawman
utterances.text: People who work from home can't take calls.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Lawman
utterances.text: And students like me can't focus on homework.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Lawman
utterances.text: People complain to their elected officials for years, but complaints are easy to dismiss without numbers behind them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Lawman
utterances.text: So I built a system to collect those numbers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Lawman
utterances.text: It's called HeliTracker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Lawman
utterances.text: This is a microphone connected to a small, inexpensive computer called the Raspberry Pi.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Lawman
utterances.text: It listens for the sound of a helicopter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Lawman
utterances.text: When it hears one, it checks Flight Radar 24 to identify the aircraft.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Lawman
utterances.text: who it's registered to, where it took off from, its altitude, its speed, and its direction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Lawman
utterances.text: It also records how loud it was.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Lawman
utterances.text: Every flight is logged, so over weeks and months, you can see patterns in which operators are the repeat offenders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Lawman
utterances.text: That data has already been useful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Lawman
utterances.text: I shared it with Congressman George Latimer, and his office raised the issue with the FAA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Lawman
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Lawman
utterances.text: Handel reached out because Waterside Plaza has the same problem with seaplanes and helicopters along the East River.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Lawman
utterances.text: I'm now adapting the system to recognize seaplanes

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Lawman
utterances.text: and we're looking at installing sensors near Waterside so residents there can have the same kind of record.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Lawman
utterances.text: I'm hopeful that with the data we collect, we'll be able to find a solution with the help of the City Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Lawman

chapters.summary: The Waterside Tenants Association president says 250,000 residents live along the East River and 2,412 seaplane operations occurred in one 2022 period; pilots use visual flight rules and she demands an independent safety review.
chapters.title: Janet Handel describes seaplane safety gaps at Waterside

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: Janet?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: My name is Janet Handel and I'm president of the Waterside Tenants Association representing the 4,000 people who live directly in front of the East River Seaplane Corridor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: When I moved to Waterside Plaza in the 70s, the Queens Brooklyn waterfront was industrial and low-lying.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: Today, the river has changed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: The population has changed, the traffic has changed, but the rules have not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: Over 250,000 people now live along this waterfront.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: NYC Ferry operates over 150 vessel trips down the East River Corridor daily, sharing the river with commercial ships, seaplanes, and helicopters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: Two schools adjacent to the Skyport serve 1,700 students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: And over one three-month period in 2022, there were 2,412 seaplane landings and takeoffs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: Yet the FAA regulations governing the Skyport go back decades.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: The safety gaps are sobering.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: This stretch of the East River is excluded from air traffic control.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: Pilots operate under visual flight rules only.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: That means helicopters, that means everything, visual flight rules.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: They must see and avoid a chaotic web of ferries and helicopters on their own in an increasingly congested corridor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: We cannot even verify if the organization identified in the regulation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: to vet pilots exists anymore, and whether pilots are adequately qualified to operate in these challenging conditions and to comply with noise restrictions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: Residents regularly observe seaplanes taking off and landing closer than the required thousand feet to our shore, bringing aircraft dangerously close to our residential buildings and dramatically increasing the sound that we're experiencing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: The seasonal noise is relentless.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: Engine roars and low frequency vibrations shake our windows, diminish residents'quality of life, and disrupt teaching.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: So we must ask, who is in charge?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: Who is protecting the 250,000 New Yorkers living along the waterfront?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: Who investigates violations, and what sanctions are imposed when operators break the rules.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: For years, we have raised these concerns with the FAA, EDC, and DOC NYC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: We need clear answers, not another handoff between agencies and organizations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: We demand an immediate independent safety review, transparent accountability,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: meaningful enforcement, and modernized oversight reflecting today's waterfront.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: Public safety cannot depend on voluntary compliance and hope.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: We should not have to wait for a tragedy to happen before someone takes responsibility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: A Waterside resident says the waterfront transformed from industrial to residential; the July hard landing and close calls with ferries and the power plant show seaplanes are unsafe; no reevaluation in decades.
chapters.title: Diane Park says seaplanes no longer appropriate on East River

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: The first seaplanes began

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: operating on the East River and docking at East 23rd Street in the late 1930s.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: At that time, the waterfront on both sides of the river was almost exclusively industrial and maritime in character.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: Since then, the river between the Ed Koch and Williamsburg bridges, where the Blaines take off and land, has dramatically transformed into a heavily congested residential corridor

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: filled with apartment buildings, schools, parks, waterfront esplanades, and ferry terminals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: It is no longer safe or appropriate for seaplanes to operate at this location.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: We at Waterside have been saying for years that these seaplanes are an accident waiting to happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: Just this past July, a seaplane had a hard landing in the East River, not too far from the ferry terminal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: Fortunately, no one was killed, but we have repeatedly watched seaplanes land dangerously close to ferries,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: take off and land right next to Waterside Plaza, fly dangerously close to the Con Edison Power Plant, to name just a few of the many dangerous maneuvers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: In the environmental review for the Domino Sugar Factory redevelopment in Williamsburg, in a section called Domino Sugar Factory Towers are a Hazard to Air Navigation on the East River,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: then director of aviation for a seaplane company operating there protested the new Domino Sugar Towers, indicating that the new towers would make the seaplane landing corridor narrower and less suitable under

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: certain wind conditions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: That was in 2007.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: There has been significantly more buildup on the East River since then.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: The FAA specifically mentions mechanical turbulence, which can be caused by large structures such as buildings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: And as far as we can tell at Waterside, there has not been an analysis or reevaluation in decades, if ever, to determine the safety of seaplanes operating at this location, given the dramatic changes in the landscape.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: What are we waiting for?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: Mass casualties?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Lawman
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: A Waterside resident says noise disrupts homes and schools; she recorded 97 decibels and notes WHO/EPA recommend 55 outside schools; there is no evidence noise abatement is enforced.
chapters.title: Miriam Applebaum describes seaplane noise impacts on health and schools

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Applebaum
utterances.text: My name is Miriam Applebaum.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Applebaum
utterances.text: I live in Waterside Plaza overlooking the East River.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Applebaum
utterances.text: And although I love my apartment from early April to the end of October, I often dread being there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Applebaum
utterances.text: The constant onslaught of seaplane landies taking off and docking is extremely noisy and stressful, disrupting my family's quiet enjoyment of our home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Applebaum
utterances.text: The noise has a serious impact on the physical and mental health of the residents of Waterside, adjacent Stuyvesant Town, and Peter Cooper, our surrounding community, and across the river in Brooklyn and Queens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Applebaum
utterances.text: The British International School and the UN International School have reported that the noise from these seaplanes disrupts classroom instruction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Applebaum
utterances.text: The WHO and EPA recommend that the level of noise outside schools should be no more than 55 decibels.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Applebaum
utterances.text: However, I and other tenants more than 350 feet from the site of Waterside on the higher floors have recorded decibels as high as 97.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Applebaum
utterances.text: Using NYC Noise, a free app from the New York Department of Environmental Protection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Applebaum
utterances.text: We can only imagine what the noise levels are at the actual schools, which are right next to the seaplane dock.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Applebaum
utterances.text: Constant exposure to loud noise is a health and learning problem for these children.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Applebaum
utterances.text: The problem has recently intensified, especially since

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Applebaum
utterances.text: Planes frequently fly closer than 1,000 feet from shore, making the noise level even worse.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Applebaum
utterances.text: We have no evidence that the noise abatement at the seaplane seaport dock is being monitored or enforced.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Applebaum
utterances.text: Why not at least do that, or better yet, stop the planes from flying at this location altogether?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Waterfront Alliance supports NYC Ferry expansion and Intros 1032, 704, and 846; it seeks clarity on DOT versus EDC for Willets Point and will submit full testimony.
chapters.title: Tyler Taba of Waterfront Alliance supports ferry expansion bills

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: Waterfront Alliance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: Oh, I forgot to give my name.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: I don't know if I need to put that for my testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: Oh, Diane Park, P-A-R-K.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Taba
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Maloney, Majority Leader Abreu, Councilmember Farias, Councilmember Thomas Henry, and all the other councilmembers who are here for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Taba
utterances.text: My name is Tyler Taba.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Taba
utterances.text: I'm the Director of Policy and Government Affairs at the Waterfront Alliance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Taba
utterances.text: Before the establishment of the NYC Ferry in 2017, Waterfront Alliance organized a series of events and white papers on how to bring back the Five Borough Ferry Service.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Taba
utterances.text: We are a big supporter of the New York City Ferry and continue to encourage the city to envision the ferry as part of its climate, transportation, and economic development goals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Taba
utterances.text: Our testimony today builds on our longstanding advocacy and support of the New York City Ferry, particularly also on our 2024 Oversight Hearing Testimony, which we refer to as the five E's of NYC Ferry, expansion, economics, electrification, emergency services, and equity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Taba
utterances.text: Our full testimony will be submitted shortly after this hearing and touches on all of those things, but for our verbal testimony today, Waterfront Alliance would like to focus on expansion.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Taba
utterances.text: We envision several new routes that would serve New Yorkers with newer, greener, and faster transit options and would reshape transportation in the region.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Taba
utterances.text: We support the bills discussed today, which look to expand ferry service to neighborhoods that would greatly benefit from waterborne transportation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Taba
utterances.text: Starting with Councilmember Farias'intro 1032, we've long supported city islanders in their advocacy for a ferry landing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Taba
utterances.text: It's great to see many community residents and partners and leaders here today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Taba
utterances.text: As has been stated, transportation to and from the island is an ongoing challenge and public transportation options are limited.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Taba
utterances.text: We support and encourage the council to support this legislation and pass it swiftly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Taba
utterances.text: so the one-year study can commence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Taba
utterances.text: We also support Councilmember Narciso's Intro 704.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Taba
utterances.text: We've supported local organizers on establishing a Canarsie Ferry going back to 2017, and also glad to see resident leaders in the community here support that as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Taba
utterances.text: We also support Councilmember Thomas Henry's Intro 846.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Taba
utterances.text: As has been discussed, Willits Point has seen tremendous transfer...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Taba
utterances.text: transformation, excuse me, and all of this new development alongside existing rich and cultural entertainment opportunities nearby.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Taba
utterances.text: We generally support ferry service here, but also seek clarity on why DOT rather than EDC, and would be happy to chat more about that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Taba
utterances.text: Of course, didn't make it in time, so I'll just conclude by saying thank you again for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Taba
utterances.text: We'll submit our full testimony into the record and look forward to working with the council.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I want to acknowledge that Councilmember Dinowitz joined us.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And I do have some questions for this panel who has experienced a lot of the concerns that we were addressing before about noise, flight takeoffs that are closer to the shoreline.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: We heard that Doc NYC is responsible for enforcing the SOP and contract.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: But have you seen examples of these violations living right there at Waterside Plaza?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And if anyone would be able to elaborate a bit more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: One thing I wanted to point out is I foiled the SOP from EDC, and the one that they provided to me was from 2013.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: I don't even know if they've evaluated their own processes in more than a decade.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: But we all have observed significant violations of seaplanes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: We have repeatedly contacted NYC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: In fact, we've been trying to have another meeting with them, and they just keep pushing us off.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: We've seen seaplanes fly dangerously close, as I said in my testimony, to boats.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: There was the annual jet ski invasion that they have on the East River, where there are hundreds of jet skis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: A seaplane landed literally right next to the jet ski.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: And as I said in my testimony, with the mechanical turbulence, buildings are blocking the wind.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: So these planes cannot necessarily land precisely where they want to land.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: And one of the photos shows the seaplane landing right next to these jet skis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: We've seen seaplanes fly over the 59th Street Bridge.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: EDC said, oh, they fly in from the south.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: That is absolutely not true.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: They generally fly in from the north.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: What they've been doing lately is they fly in from the north, and then they turn around over Manhattan or Brooklyn and Queens, and then they land in the river.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: Now they're trying to land more towards the Brooklyn and Queens side.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: But there are multiple violations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: I don't know if you want to add to this, Janet.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: Okay, turn it on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: The point that I wanted to...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: make that, and I just want to show you this video.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: This is showing a seaplane that landed right by the ferry, very close, and then there it is coming up against the jet ski invasion.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: I mean, that is like...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: How is that safe?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: And if you can see the photo of the actual, there's a photo that follows of where the plane actually landed, and it will show you that it's unreal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: Yeah, and I guess this raises the question that we have, and I would just say we have found this out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: So this plane is in the wake of that ferry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: The plane that the July 5th accident happened because of the NTSB final ruling said it was a hard hit of a wake, and that hard hit caused the thing to collapse.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: So what is the seaplane doing in the wake of a ferry?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: And to think that you're going to be able to land in the East River without wakes with the amount of ferry traffic and the commercial barges that are going up and down, it's a very, very complex environment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: And that leads us again to this issue when we look at it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: The FAA regulation has three components.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: Two of them have to do with ceilings and so forth and daytime operations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: The third component is subsumed into the FAA regulation, but it is not an FAA-issued regulation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: That is the part that has to do with...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: Our Skyport 6NR, that is locally generated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: It's the same, you know, for every city that has an airport.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: The city says, we're the local area and we lay out the rules for our city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: That's where the thousand foot rule is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: And that's where also the rule is that the seaplane operators must

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: be vetted by the Northeast Seaplane Pilots Association, which nobody can find.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: Maybe it existed once upon a time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: It does not exist today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: We don't know that there's anybody, any vetting going on of these seaplane pilots other than

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: whatever the FAA does for seaplane pilots in general, but nothing about the East River exclusion zone so that they have skilled landing in the East River.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: And what really brought this to mind is we recently, over the last summer, we saw a new operator that we had not seen before that has, their tail is blue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: And they seem to be more, that have more of the bad operations, landing closer to our buildings, not observing the rules.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: And that makes me question, you know, do they, you know, they haven't operated here before, maybe they're inexperienced, but, you know,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: We live there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: You know, we're very mindful of the crash where Corey Little crashed his plane into the Bel Air on the Upper East Side.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: I mean, when we are, I've been in Diane's apartment and I see the seaplanes coming down.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: It looks like it is coming right at you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: And then it turns off.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: It's unnerving.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: And we see no evidence that Doc NYC is monitoring anything, whether it's safety, whether it's noise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: This is all talk that they're doing, but there is no evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: And it would be great if you could push them on that, their measurements and how they're monitoring, because we don't see anything like that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: It would be interesting to see what the incident reports are, or what are the operating reports that they submit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: What do they require if somebody, you know, a Joe seaplane operator decides he wants to open up a business and start landing there, you know, what do they require of them?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: We don't know any of that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: There's one photo in this carousel, which is kids playing at school and the seaplanes landing right next to where these kids are in school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: I mean, we know they're dangerous.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: We've seen many, many dangerous maneuvers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: I've seen planes taking off right next to the schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: I mean, this is crazy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: And then the noise from these planes, you know, affecting instruction for these children.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you for so clearly articulating some of the violations that you've seen and for submitting the visual testimony, which really brings it to life here.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: What is the mechanism for reporting these incidents?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And how do you report them when you see these violations?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: I mean, we've tried to communicate with EDC, you know, and DOC NYC, but they're very off-putting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Diane Park
utterances.text: It's not that they're open to accepting what we're trying to explain to them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: We tried to schedule meetings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: We have had a couple of meetings with elected officials and EDC and DOC NYC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: But usually they try and say, we want to, you know, we're gathering information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
utterances.text: We want to have the meeting at a later time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Handel
